articles.title: Global nuclear warhead count rises for the first time in years
articles.body:
- SIPRI estimates the world held about 12,187 nuclear warheads in January 2026, with roughly 9,745 in military stockpiles and 4,012 deployed on missiles and at bomber bases.
- All nine nuclear-armed states expanded or modernized their arsenals in 2025, even as total warhead numbers kept falling due to US and Russian dismantlement of retired weapons.
The world’s nine nuclear-armed states expanded their arsenals in 2025, according to a new assessment from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. Researchers Hans M. Kristensen and Matt Korda found that most countries deployed new nuclear-armed or nuclear-capable weapons during the year, even as the overall number of warheads in the world continued to decline.
SIPRI counted an estimated 12,187 nuclear warheads worldwide as of January 2026. About 9,745 of those sit in military stockpiles ready for potential use, roughly 130 more than a year earlier. An estimated 4,012 warheads were deployed on missiles and at bomber bases, an increase of about 100 from January 2025. SIPRI attributes much of that rise to a reassessment of Russian deployments and new estimates of Chinese and Indian warheads placed with operational forces.
The total figure keeps falling only because the United States and Russia are dismantling retired weapons faster than new ones are built elsewhere. Both countries still hold more than 1,000 retired warheads awaiting dismantlement. SIPRI’s researchers say the pace of dismantlement appears to be slowing, and it may soon fall behind the rate at which new warheads enter global stockpiles.
The United States and Russia together hold about 83 percent of the world’s deployable warheads and nearly 86 percent of the total inventory, though that share has been shrinking slightly each year as other arsenals grow. Both countries are running extensive modernization programs covering their delivery systems, warheads and production infrastructure, and both have been hit by delays and cost overruns. The U.S. Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile program is running at least four years late and roughly 81 percent over its original cost estimate, according to the report. Russia’s Sarmat heavy ICBM is more than eight years behind schedule, and a 2025 test reportedly damaged its launch infrastructure.
China’s arsenal grew from about 600 warheads to roughly 620 over the year and is expected to keep expanding through the next decade. India’s stockpile rose slightly to about 190 warheads, while Pakistan held steady at around 170. North Korea is believed to have assembled about 60 warheads, though SIPRI says it may have enough fissile material for at least 90. Israel’s stockpile is estimated at 90 warheads, unchanged from the previous year. Britain’s declared warhead count held at 225, though the government has said it plans to raise that ceiling to 260 and has stopped publicly disclosing deployment details. France’s stockpile stayed near 290 warheads.
One factor complicating outside estimates: the 2010 New START treaty between the U.S. and Russia expired without replacement in February 2026, cutting off a longstanding source of official data on American and Russian strategic deployments. SIPRI says nuclear-armed states in general are becoming less transparent about their arsenals, making independent verification harder across the board.
The report also points to shifts in how countries plan to use these weapons. Russia’s 2024 doctrine update widened the circumstances under which Moscow says it could use nuclear weapons, a change SIPRI links to the war in Ukraine. Belarus has said Russian nuclear weapons are stationed on its territory, and Russia has shown video of its Oreshnik missile, which can carry conventional or nuclear warheads, operating inside the country.
In Europe, Britain and France signed the Northwood Declaration in July 2025, agreeing their nuclear forces could be coordinated in response to an extreme threat to Europe. Britain also announced plans to buy F-35A aircraft and rejoin NATO’s nuclear-sharing mission, which would make it the sixth NATO host nation for U.S. nuclear weapons. Poland, Finland and Sweden have all discussed hosting U.S. nuclear weapons in some capacity in recent years.
China’s expanding missile force, meanwhile, has drawn attention for a possible shift away from its historic practice of storing warheads separately from launchers. The Pentagon has assessed that China loaded more than 100 missiles into three new silo fields in 2025, though there’s no public evidence the missiles are armed. SIPRI estimates China may have deployed a small number of warheads, perhaps up to 34, with operational forces as of January 2026.
South Asia saw its own escalation risk in 2025. India and Pakistan fought their most serious armed conflict in decades in May, involving Indian strikes on Pakistani bases assessed to have nuclear missions. Both sides avoided crossing into nuclear territory, but SIPRI describes the clash as a shift in regional dynamics that leaves the risk of rapid escalation as an ongoing concern.

articles.title: Russia’s Deployed Nuclear Warheads Hit Post-2017 High
articles.body:
Russia has expanded the number of operational nuclear warheads deployed on delivery systems for a fourth consecutive year, bringing its deployed total to the highest level since 2017, according to the annual World Nuclear Forces report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
As of January 2026, Russia possessed an estimated total inventory of 5,420 nuclear warheads. Of that total, 2,604 warheads were held in central storage, 1,020 were retired and awaiting dismantlement, and 1,796 were operationally deployed on ballistic missiles and strategic bombers.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to SIPRI data, Russia’s deployed arsenal has grown incrementally since 2022, rising from 1,588 operational warheads in 2022 to 1,674 in 2023, 1,710 in 2024, 1,718 in 2025, and 1,796 in early 2026. The current deployed figure represents an approximate 14% increase compared to 2020 levels.
By comparison, the US maintained an estimated 1,770 deployed warheads over the same timeframe out of an overall stockpile comparable with that of Russia. Among other declared nuclear-weapon states, France maintained 280 deployed warheads, while the United Kingdom deployed 120.
China increased its deployed warheads from 24 to 34 out of an estimated total inventory of 620 warheads. India also initiated operational sea-based nuclear deployments aboard ballistic missile submarines, maintaining approximately 12 deployed warheads in 2025 from a total arsenal estimated at 190 weapons.
Drones Strike Taganrog Airfield and Tolyatti Chemical Plant
Triad distribution and dispersal of strategic bombers
According to the institute’s breakdown, Russian ground-based Strategic Rocket Forces account for up to 1,092 operational warheads, with roughly 892 deployed on intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs).
Russia’s naval triad comprises 13 strategic nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines (SSBNs) capable of carrying up to 928 warheads. With two submarines undergoing long-term maintenance and overhaul, SIPRI estimated that approximately 704 submarine-launched warheads are currently available for operational deployment.
An estimated 586 nuclear warheads are allocated to the Russian Aerospace Forces’ strategic long-range aviation. SIPRI noted that following precision strikes by Ukrainian forces against Russian military airbases in 2025, the Russian military dispersed a significant portion of its Tu-160 and Tu-95MS strategic bombers to remote northern and eastern facilities, including the Belaya, Dyagilevo, and Olenya airfields.
While global aggregate warhead counts continue to decrease gradually as retired Cold War-era weapons are dismantled, SIPRI researchers highlighted that the number of ready, operationally deployed warheads is climbing across several nuclear-armed powers, assessing that the upward trend is likely to persist over the coming years.
Kremlin nuclear signaling against European neighbors
The SIPRI findings coincide with intensified nuclear rhetoric from Moscow directed at NATO member states in Eastern and Northern Europe.
On Friday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned that Lithuania would be targeted by Russian nuclear systems if Vilnius proceeds with constitutional amendments lifting its ban on hosting foreign nuclear weapons.
“If there are nuclear weapons on the territory that are aimed at us, then the territory of this country will also be in the sights of our nuclear weapons,” Peskov stated on Russian state television.
The warning followed a 7-2 vote on Wednesday, Sept. 9, by Lithuania’s parliamentary Committee on Legal Affairs to advance draft constitutional revisions, with a definitive legislative vote scheduled for early 2027.
The measure would establish the legal authority for NATO allies to deploy nuclear capabilities to Lithuanian soil during crisis scenarios.
Regional security tensions have grown since Russia began stationing tactical nuclear weapons in neighboring Belarus in June 2023. In December 2025, Moscow deployed its intermediate-range ballistic missile (IRBM) system, designated Oreshnik, to Belarusian territory following its initial combat use against targets in Ukraine, while Russian and Belarusian forces carried out joint tactical nuclear exercises in May.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia targets Kyiv gas stations for second day
articles.body:
Key developments on Sept. 11:
- 'There might be nothing left tomorrow' — Russia ramps up attacks on Kyiv's gas stations
- Canada sanctions 8 individuals over deportation, militarization of Ukrainian children
- Ukrainian Flamingo missiles strike chemical plant in Russia's Volgograd, Fire Point says
- Russian forces executed 2 Ukrainian POWs near Dobropillia, prosecutors say
- 'The time has come' — Belarus's Lukashenko inspects troops, says army 'needs shaking up'
- Ukrainian drones hit oil refinery, Ozon warehouse as Russia's Saratov comes under attack
Russian drones struck two gas stations in Kyiv on Sept. 11, killing two people and injuring 12 others, including a child, local authorities said.
An air raid siren sounded in the capital at around 9:10 a.m. local time. About half an hour later, explosions were heard across the city, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Five people were hospitalized, while one was treated at the scene, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. At 11:45 a.m. local time, Klitschko said two of the injured had died in the hospital.
The number of people injured rose to 12 by around 3 p.m. local time, including a 12-year-old boy, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) said.
As of 3 p.m. local time, seven people remained hospitalized, according to the mayor.
One emergency responder was among the injured in the Russian attacks on the gas stations, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
Artem, 25, a refueling technician who asked to be identified by his first name only, said the station previously closed only during "red-level" air raid alerts, which signal a potential missile attack. Following a series of strikes on the city, the station also began closing during "yellow-level" alerts on Sept. 11, which indicate a drone attack, he added.
Artem added that amid the recent attacks, customers have also started buying more fuel, filling their car tanks and storing additional gasoline in personal jerry cans.
"It's scary that there might be nothing left tomorrow," the refueling technician said.
A Russian drone hit an office building in the Podilskyi district, damaging the building and starting a fire on the fourth floor, while a neighboring one-story non-residential building also caught fire, Klitschko said.
Another Russian drone struck the same office building again in a seperate attack hours later at around 6:50 p.m., according to Klitschko. As a result of this strike, a nearby warehouse caught fire, Klitschko said.
The Sept. 11 attacks came as Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski arrived at Kyiv's main train station. The exact agenda of his visit is not known, but it comes amid growing tensions between Poland and Ukraine.

Canada sanctions 8 individuals over deportation, militarization of Ukrainian children
Canada has sanctioned eight individuals involved in Russia's unlawful deportation, indoctrination and militarization of Ukrainian children, the Ukrainian Bring Kids Back UA initiative told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 11.
The sanctions entered into force on Sept. 4 and were announced during President Volodymyr Zelensky's visit to Canada.
The sanctioned individuals include Russian officials, youth movement leaders, and occupation officials accused of facilitating the abduction of Ukrainian children from Russian-occupied territories and their integration into Russia's education system.
Crucially, the list of sanctioned individuals goes beyond deportation and targets those who abducted Ukrainian children, but also those who run the system of their re-education, Maksym Maksymov, head of Bring Kids Back UA, told the Kyiv Independent.
The list included Grigory Gurov, head of Russia's Federal Agency for Youth Affairs and former chairman of the board of the Movement of the First, a Russian state-led youth organization, Artur Orlov, chairman of the board of the Movement of the First, and Denis Chornobay, head of the movement's regional branch in occupied Donetsk.
"These are the people responsible for programs of indoctrination and militarisation — for ensuring that Ukrainian children cease to identify as Ukrainians and ultimately end up in the Russian army," Maksymov said.
read also
Ukrainian Flamingo missiles strike chemical plant in Russia's Volgograd, Fire Point says
Ukraine carried out an FP-5 "Flamingo" missile strike on Russian military-industrial facilities in Volgograd overnight on Sept. 11, according to Ukrainian missile manufacturer Fire Point.
"Flamingos paid a little visit to Volgograd last night," Fire Point said in a social media statement. "Ukrainian sanctions, as always, proved to be the most effective."
The company said direct hits on the facilities sparked a "massive fire."
The FP-5 Flamingo is a Ukrainian heavy cruise missile manufactured by Fire Point that first entered service in August 2025. While early versions were relatively inaccurate, the missile has since undergone modifications and upgrades and has been used in several attacks on Russian military-industrial facilities.
"The Flamingo was fairly inaccurate in the beginning," Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent, explaining that Fire Point has since modified and upgraded the missile. "The missile is now operationally more useful," he said.
Footage posted by monitoring channels on social media showed fires apparently coming from the facility, although the extent of the damage remained unclear.
Volgograd Region Governor Andrey Bocharov acknowledged that a Ukrainian missile strike had taken place in the city, claiming that "an industrial facility in southern Volgograd" was damaged by "falling debris."

Russian forces executed 2 Ukrainian POWs near Dobropillia, prosecutors say
Russian troops shot dead two Ukrainian prisoners of war (POWs) in an execution near the eastern city of Dobropillia on Sept. 2, the Donetsk Oblast Prosecutor's Office said on Sept. 11.
According to the pretrial investigation, the two National Guard soldiers were carrying out a combat mission at a position in a forest belt near Dobropillia, Donetsk Oblast, when Russian soldiers captured them.
The Russian troops then allegedly shot the Ukrainian servicemen with automatic weapons, prosecutors said.
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) is investigating the case under Article 438 of Ukraine's Criminal Code, which covers war crimes resulting in death.
Investigators are carrying out urgent investigative measures to establish the circumstances of the incident and identify the Russian servicemen allegedly involved, the prosecutor's office said.
The execution of prisoners of war is prohibited under the Geneva Conventions and constitutes a war crime.

'The time has come' — Belarus's Lukashenko inspects troops, says army 'needs shaking up'
Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenko announced the continued inspection of Belarus' armed forces for readiness, the state-owned Belarusian news agency BelTA said on Sept. 11.
"I've already said it in plain terms: the army needs shaking up, the time has come. The whole army. We'll check everyone. Up to mobilization," Lukashenko said.
Currently, an artillery brigade and communications units are being checked for readiness, after tank and motor rifle units had already been inspected, according to Lukashenko.
"We are preparing for war so that there won't be one," he said.
The tests should resemble actual battles to prepare the Belarusian troops properly, according to the dictator.
"These are the lessons of the special military operation," Lukashenko added, referring to Russia's full-scale invasion.
Lukashenko also said that his youngest son, Nikolai Lukashenko, was currently serving in the army as a lieutenant after being drafted, without revealing the unit where he serves.
read also
Ukrainian drones hit oil refinery, Ozon warehouse as Russia's Saratov comes under attack
Ukrainian drones struck the Russian city of Saratov overnight on Sept. 11, hitting a local oil refinery and a logistics hub operated by e-commerce giant Ozon, according to Ukraine's General Staff and satellite imagery published by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL).
Videos circulating on social media appeared to show drones and Russian air defenses in operation in the region.
The attack on an oil refinery owned by Russian energy giant Rosneft sparked a fire at the facility, Ukraine's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Saratov Oblast Governor Roman Busargin posted on Telegram around 2 a.m. local time about a threat from unmanned aerial vehicles, claiming that emergency services had been placed on full alert.
Soon after the strike on the refinery, a logistics hub belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Ozon was also reported to be set ablaze in Saratov. Video published by Exilenova+ appeared to show a major fire emanating from the facility shortly after explosions were heard.
Satellite imagery published later in the day by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) showed the Ozon warehouse had been completely gutted by fire following the Ukrainian attack. The logistics center covers 100,000 square meters.
"Good results from our long-range strikes aimed at reducing Russia’s capacity to wage war. An enterprise and an oil industry facility were hit in the Saratov and Volgograd regions…Thank you to everyone who is developing Ukraine’s strength so that there will be no safe havens left in Russia for anything that supports the war," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 11.

articles.title: All the Pentagon’s men
articles.body:
All the Pentagon’s men
The Iran war and a crisis of command in the US: what do 12 departures mean?
TEHRAN — Since the beginning of the war against Iran, Donald Trump and his Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, have repeatedly described the performance of US forces and the results of American military operations in glowing terms, using phrases such as “victory,” “historic success,” and “major military achievements.”
According to the administration’s narrative, US operations have been carried out with overwhelming force, their intended targets have been hit, and American forces have demonstrated their superiority on the battlefield. The picture presented by the White House and the Pentagon is that of a highly capable, disciplined, and tightly controlled military machine operating in full coordination with the administration.
But alongside that narrative, another important reality has emerged, one that receives far less attention in the political messaging: sweeping changes at the highest levels of the US military and national security establishment.
Under Pete Hegseth, a significant number of generals, admirals, and senior civilian officials at the Pentagon have been fired, pushed into early retirement, resigned, or otherwise removed from their positions under unexpected circumstances. These changes have not been limited to mid-level commanders. They have reached some of the most senior positions in the US military, including the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the chief of naval operations, senior Army commanders, Air Force leaders, the head of US Special Operations Command, the head of Cyber Command, and the director of the Defense Intelligence Agency.
The significance of this development lies not only in the number of people who have left their positions. The timing of these departures is equally important. Some of the changes took place before the war with Iran. Others came amid the escalating tensions with Tehran and in the period immediately preceding military operations. Still others occurred while the United States was already engaged in a full-scale war and extensive military operations in the Middle East.
Some of these dismissals came without any clear official explanation. In several cases, the Pentagon simply cited a “loss of confidence.” In others, the officials were removed without any public explanation at all. Reports in the US media have also pointed to disagreements over military strategy, force management, the war in Ukraine, Middle East operations, the future structure of the Army, weapons production, and even how the United States should deal with Iran. One of the most significant examples was the removal of Defense Intelligence Agency Director Gen. Jeffrey Kruse, who was dismissed shortly after a controversial intelligence assessment questioned the extent of the damage inflicted on Iran’s nuclear program.
The departures of senior commanders during the war have raised even more questions. Gen. Randy George, the Army’s top officer, was forced into retirement in April 2026 while the United States was actively fighting Iran. At the same time, Gen. David Hodne and Gen. William Green were also removed.
During the same period, Navy Secretary John Phelan left his post. Several months later, Army Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll resigned amid reports of deep disagreements with Hegseth over the future of the Army, its structural transformation, and the repeated removal of senior commanders.
When a large number of senior military and national security officials are replaced within a relatively short period, the pattern itself becomes an important sign of instability, internal disagreements, and profound changes inside the Pentagon.
Of course, these departures do not all tell the same story. Some officials were directly fired, others were pressured into early retirement, and some resigned. In certain cases, no clear official reason was ever provided. In others, disagreements over the future of the military, modernization plans, Hegseth’s policies, or intelligence assessments concerning Iran appear to have played a role.
The following list is intended to provide a broader picture of what has been happening inside the US military and national security establishment during the Trump-Hegseth era. It helps distinguish between the administration’s official narrative of “victory and success” and the more complicated reality inside the Pentagon, marked by leadership changes, strategic disagreements, personnel turmoil, concerns over ammunition supplies, and political pressure.
1. Gen. Randy George, Chief of Staff of the Army
Gen. Randy George was one of the most experienced senior officers in the US Army. A career infantry officer, he served in the Persian Gulf War as well as in Iraq and Afghanistan. Before becoming Army chief, he held a number of senior command positions and also served as the senior military assistant to Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin. He ultimately rose to become the Army’s highest-ranking officer.
But on April 2, 2026, roughly five weeks after the war with Iran began, Hegseth asked George to step down and take immediate retirement. The decision came as the United States was actively engaged in the war with Iran and the Army was carrying out extensive military operations in the region. A US official told CBS that Hegseth wanted someone who would implement his and Trump’s vision for the future of the Army. After his departure, George told Army personnel that American soldiers deserved leaders who were courageous and had character.
2. Gen. Christopher Donahue, Commander of US Army Europe and Africa
Gen. Christopher Donahue was one of the most prominent commanders of his generation. A Special Forces officer and West Point graduate, he commanded the 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta and the 82nd Airborne Division. He became widely known as the last American soldier to board a C-17 during the US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021. He later became commander of US Army Europe and Africa and commander of NATO land forces.
 
 Donahue left his command in July 2026, while the war with Iran was still underway, after only about 18 months in the position. Reports indicated that Hegseth had become dissatisfied with him and that efforts to extend his tenure did not succeed. Donahue had also been involved in efforts to apply lessons from Ukraine’s drone warfare to the modernization of the US Army, a subject that later became part of broader disagreements over the Army’s transformation. His departure, only months after Randy George was removed and while the Iran war was still ongoing, became another major sign of the sweeping changes at the top of the Army.
3. Gen. David Hodne, Commander of Army Training and Transformation
Gen. David Hodne was a senior Army commander responsible for a structure that played a major role in training, preparing, and transforming US ground forces for future wars. His position was particularly important at a time when the Army was reconsidering its force structure and moving toward greater reliance on drones, unmanned systems, and emerging technologies.
 
 Hodne was removed in April 2026, at the same time Randy George was pushed out and while the United States was fighting Iran. No specific official reason was given for his removal. But the timing was significant: three senior Army leaders were removed at roughly the same time, as the United States was engaged in war and as Hegseth was pushing major changes to the Army’s future structure and leadership.
4. Gen. William Green Jr., Chief of the Army Chaplain Corps
Gen. William Green Jr. headed the US Army Chaplain Corps, the organization responsible for providing religious services and spiritual support to soldiers and military families. His position may have been less visible than that of the Army chief, but his removal from office was significant because it demonstrated how broadly Hegseth’s changes extended across the military establishment.
 
 Green was also removed in April 2026, during the war with Iran, and the Pentagon did not provide a specific explanation for the decision. Hegseth had previously criticized the Chaplain Corps, accusing it of being influenced by “political correctness” and “secular humanism.” Green’s removal on the same day as the departures of George and Hodne reinforced the perception that Hegseth’s reshaping of the military was not limited to operational commanders at the very top, but extended across different parts of the Army’s institutional structure.
5. Gen. James Mingus, Vice Chief of Staff of the Army
Gen. James Mingus was a senior Army officer with extensive experience in military operations and command. He served for roughly two years as the Army’s vice chief of staff, making him one of the most senior figures in the Army’s internal leadership structure.
 
 Mingus eventually left the position and formally retired on February 6, 2026. Reports during the Hegseth era indicated that he had been pressured toward early retirement as Hegseth sought to reshape the Army’s senior leadership. Unlike Randy George, however, Mingus left before the war with Iran began. His successor, Lt. Gen. Christopher LaNeve, was confirmed for the position in January 2026 and was viewed as more closely aligned with Hegseth’s approach.
6. John Phelan, Secretary of the Navy
John Phelan was a civilian official appointed by the Trump administration to serve as Secretary of the Navy. He was responsible for overseeing the Navy’s civilian leadership, including major issues involving shipbuilding and fleet expansion. His position became particularly important as the Trump administration promised to increase US naval power and dramatically expand the production of warships.
 
 Phelan left his position in April 2026, while the war with Iran was underway. Trump later said Phelan had struggled to work effectively with others and that disagreements had emerged over the Navy’s shipbuilding program. Hegseth personally informed him that he was being removed. His departure, alongside the removal of several senior Army commanders during the war, showed that the shake-up at the Pentagon was not limited to uniformed officers but also extended into the civilian leadership of the Defense Department.
7. Daniel P. Driscoll, Secretary of the Army
Daniel P. Driscoll was one of the senior civilian officials overseeing the Army and was closely involved in efforts to reshape the service for future warfare. His modernization agenda, developed alongside Randy George, included greater use of drones and unmanned systems, changes to Army formations, and the retirement of some older equipment. The goal was to prepare the Army for a fundamentally different kind of battlefield.
 
 Driscoll resigned on August 31, 2026, while the war with Iran was still underway. His resignation came after months of tension with Hegseth. People familiar with the matter said Driscoll had raised concerns with the Trump administration about the direction of Army transformation and the removal of senior commanders involved in shaping those reforms. By the time he resigned, Randy George and Christopher Donahue had already left the Army’s senior command structure. Driscoll’s departure therefore became one of the latest episodes in a broader leadership crisis unfolding during the Iran war.
8. Adm. Alvin Holsey, Commander of US Southern Command
Adm. Alvin Holsey was a senior Navy officer who commanded US Southern Command, or SOUTHCOM. The command is responsible for US military operations and security interests across Central and South America and the Caribbean. Holsey took command of SOUTHCOM in 2024 after more than 37 years of service in the Navy and was expected to remain in the position for several years.
 
 But in October 2025, Hegseth announced that Holsey would retire at the end of that year, well ahead of the expected end of his command. Officially, the retirement was presented as a decision by Holsey, but Reuters, citing US officials, reported that he had effectively been pushed out by Hegseth. Disagreements over the way SOUTHCOM was conducting operations in the region were also reportedly part of the dispute.
9. Lt. Gen. Douglas Sims II, Director of the Joint Staff
Lt. Gen. Douglas Sims II was a senior Army officer who served as director of the Joint Staff, a highly influential position at the center of military planning and coordination among the US armed services. His career unfolded during a period of major changes at the top of the Pentagon, and his future was affected by Hegseth’s reshaping of the senior officer corps.
 
 In Sims’ case, the key issue involved his expected promotion to four-star general. Media reports said Hegseth blocked the promotion and that Sims was investigated over possible links to leaks of classified information, allegations that were not substantiated. Senior military officials, including the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, defended Sims’ record. Hegseth was also reportedly concerned about Sims’ ties to retired Gen. Mark Milley. Sims ultimately retired from the Army in 2025.
10. Adm. Shoshana Chatfield, US Military Representative to NATO
Adm. Shoshana Chatfield was one of the Navy’s senior commanders and served as the US military representative to NATO’s Military Committee. The position is particularly important because it places its holder at the center of military coordination between the United States and its European allies. Chatfield had previously held a number of senior command and leadership positions within the Navy.
 
 In April 2025, Hegseth removed her from the position. The Pentagon officially said it had “lost confidence in her ability to lead,” but provided few additional details. The decision came during the early months of Hegseth’s tenure, when he was simultaneously reshaping senior leadership across the Army, Navy, and broader US national security establishment.
11. Gen. Jeffrey Kruse, Director of the Defense Intelligence Agency
Gen. Jeffrey Kruse headed the Defense Intelligence Agency, or DIA, the organization responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign military intelligence for the Pentagon and US military commanders. Because of that role, DIA assessments of an adversary’s military capabilities can directly influence American military and political decision-making.
 
 Kruse’s case was one of the clearest examples of Pentagon leadership changes becoming intertwined with Iran. Following the US “Midnight Hammer” operation against Iranian nuclear facilities, an initial DIA assessment reportedly concluded that the strikes had set Iran’s nuclear program back by only a matter of months, an assessment that differed sharply from the Trump administration’s much more optimistic public claims about the extent of the damage. Kruse was removed in August 2025, and multiple reports subsequently linked his departure to the controversy surrounding the intelligence assessment.
12. Joe Kent, Director of the National Counterterrorism Center
Joe Kent was a former US Army Special Forces officer who went on to become director of the National Counterterrorism Center, or NCTC, one of the most important US institutions responsible for coordinating counterterrorism efforts. He was associated with the “America First” wing of the Trump movement, and his appointment suggested that he was not simply a political opponent of the administration.
 
 But Kent became one of the most outspoken internal critics of the war with Iran. On March 17, 2026, during the third week of the war, he resigned and said he could not support the continuation of the conflict in good conscience. Kent argued that Iran did not pose an imminent threat to the United States and said he could not support sending another generation of American service members into a war he believed did not serve the interests of the American people. His resignation was one of the clearest examples of a senior Trump administration official leaving specifically because of opposition to the Iran war.
Taken together, these 12 cases paint a picture of sweeping change at the top of the US military and national security establishment. Some of these officials were removed before the war with Iran began. Others became directly associated with disputes over Iran, while still others left their positions while the United States was actively engaged in the conflict.
 
 Joe Kent’s resignation stands out because, unlike many senior officials whose reasons for leaving were never fully explained, he explicitly identified the Iran war as the reason for his departure. Jeffrey Kruse’s case, meanwhile, shows how even an intelligence assessment concerning the effectiveness of US strikes on Iran could become a highly sensitive issue inside the national security establishment.
 
 The issue, therefore, is not simply how many commanders have left the Pentagon during Hegseth’s tenure. The more important question is what these departures reveal about the stability of US military decision-making and the disagreements over the future direction of the American armed forces. When the Army chief, senior commanders, cabinet-level officials, and intelligence leaders are removed or depart within a relatively short period, it becomes difficult to dismiss the pattern as routine personnel turnover.
 
 Taken together, these developments can be seen as a sign of serious tensions, internal divisions, and structural problems within the Trump administration and the Pentagon, particularly because many of the changes have occurred while Washington is simultaneously dealing with a major war, pressure on ammunition and air-defense inventories, the need to rapidly modernize the armed forces, and disagreements over how the conflict should be managed.
The steady departure of experienced officials under such circumstances raises a broader question: Is the restructuring of the Pentagon actually producing a more unified and effective military leadership, or is the repeated removal of experienced commanders creating additional instability at a time when the United States can least afford it?
The scale, speed, and timing of these changes—especially their overlap with the Iran war—make them an important indicator of the internal difficulties facing the Trump administration and the Pentagon. The central question now is whether this sweeping reshuffling will ultimately produce a more disciplined and coherent military structure, or whether the continued departure of experienced leaders will itself become a source of deeper problems and weaker decision-making in Washington.

articles.title: Iran bags US hardware, German voters revolt, and Zelensky survives a 160 km ‘near-miss’: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
Iran bags US hardware, German voters revolt, and Zelensky survives a 160 km ‘near-miss’: RT stories that shaped the week
Gulf turns into a shooting gallery
The US-Iran conflict moved increasingly onto the water this week, with oil tankers, warships, and drones all getting involved around one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
Washington struck five Iranian crude carriers on Tuesday after previously attacking three other commercial vessels. Tehran retaliated, claiming strikes on eight tankers and two US Navy vessels, while an Iranian attack reportedly damaged several US warplanes at an airbase in Jordan.
Iran also captured an American underwater drone, and two days later, released footage of a US Saildrone surveillance vessel burning in the water.
Tehran says the Strait of Hormuz remains under its control and has announced plans for another restricted shipping zone nearby.
Oil markets react
The escalating hostilities saw Brent crude surge back above $100 a barrel this week, breaking the threshold for the first time in months.
Meanwhile, Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have added to fears of further disruption as the kingdom’s oil production in August reportedly fell to its lowest level since 1990 amid growing pressure on its usual export routes.
Trump dividend
As oil prices continue to destabilize the global energy markets, the fallout is expected to become a major issue in the upcoming US November midterm election. The US president, however, has refused to back down, promising “a lot more” strikes on Iranian tankers.
As for concerned voters, Trump promised to pay every American adult a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” if Republicans keep control of Congress. He did not explain exactly how the payouts potentially costing well over $1 trillion would be funded.
Speaking of enormous piles of money...
An RT investigation looked at Ukraine’s industrial-scale scam-call business, which is estimated to generate around $1 billion every month and employs some 60,000 people.
The business has also become entangled with allegations that corrupt Ukrainian officials have been taking protection money from the very fraudsters they were supposed to go after, leading to the resignation of Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko.
By Friday, Zelensky’s chief of staff, Kirill Budanov, was also reportedly under investigation over possible financial crimes.
Separately, the New York Times reported that Ukraine lost around $1.2 billion to fraud, waste, and mismanagement in military procurement in 2024 alone.
Washington keeps trying diplomacy
While investigators searched for Ukraine’s missing money, Washington continued looking for a peace deal. After Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kiev last weekend, Trump spoke with Putin by phone on Tuesday.
Moscow said it hopes Russia-US-Ukraine talks can resume, while Zelensky floated the UAE, Türkiye, and Switzerland as possible venues.
Talking to Russia may be catching on
While Washington has reopened direct channels with Moscow, some European governments that have spent years doing the opposite have increasingly felt the political cost at home.
The clearest example came in Germany, where the Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt last weekend, crushing Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU. Migration was a major issue, but the AfD has also campaigned against sanctions on Russia, Germany’s massive support for Kiev and the abandonment of cheap Russian energy.
Merz said he was “deeply shocked” by the result. He then announced that he would change virtually nothing.
Brussels’ response was hardly more conciliatory, with German media reporting this week that Saxony-Anhalt could lose hundreds of millions of euros in EU funding if the AfD manages to form a government and clashes with Brussels.
Similar frustration was visible in neighboring Poland, where protesters marched under the banner ‘Poland for Peace’ and accused Warsaw of “trying to turn Russophobia into our national sport” and pushing the country toward confrontation with Russia.
Public dissent grows, governments double down
None of this appears to have slowed Europe’s confrontation with Russia. Moscow this week ordered Germany’s consulate in St. Petersburg and Goethe-Institut cultural centers in Russia to close in retaliation for similar measures taken by Berlin.
Hungary’s new government, which has reversed the comparatively pragmatic Russia policy of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, expelled ten Russian diplomats. Moscow promised a “harsh and painful” response.
Lithuania, meanwhile, moved closer to scrapping its constitutional ban on hosting weapons of mass destruction, potentially opening the door to nuclear weapons being stationed in the NATO country. Moscow warned that these weapons would become Russian targets.
160km ‘near miss’
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store continued the Western ‘Russian drone’ hysteria by claiming that Vladimir Zelensky’s plane was “almost hit by a drone” while leaving Moldova. Western media duly ran with the story.
However, soon after, Moldova itself pointed out that Zelensky’s aircraft had been sitting safely on the ground, faced “no direct threat,” and that the drone eventually crashed around 160km from Chisinau airport.
Europe counts the bill
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov summed up Europe’s current approach rather dramatically, accusing the EU of committing economic harakiri by cutting itself off from Russian energy while its own citizens and industry bear the cost.
The assessment was only further proved accurate after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, one of Kiev’s strongest supporters, similarly warned on Thursday that the EU can forget about competing with China or the US after cutting itself off from cheap Russian energy.
Russia and India are doing business
While much of Europe remains focused on sanctions, diplomatic expulsions and military confrontation, Moscow and New Delhi spent the week discussing planes, trade, energy, space, and investment.
The first INNOPROM. India industrial fair opened in New Delhi, bringing together more than 120 Russian and Indian companies, with agreements covering 105 Russian Il-114-300 regional passenger aircraft and plans for local production of the SJ-100 jet in India.
Russian President Vladimir Putin visited India for talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the BRICS summit, as the two countries work toward $100 billion in bilateral trade and closer economic ties.
In other news
AI had another reassuring week as Anthropic revealed five cases in which scientists used its Claude models to help research dangerous pathogens and increase transmission of deadly viruses, which could be used to develop lethal biological weapons.
The report came days after Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger said he believes there is a greater than 10% chance AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade, while his colleague Jacob Coxon quit the company, warning that sufficiently advanced AI could one day help create “extinction-level bioweapons.”
OpenAI, meanwhile, faced new reports that its autonomous agents had once again bypassed restrictions and used outside websites to communicate with one another.
The UN, meanwhile, redrew the world this week and officially endorsed a new map that shows Africa closer to its true relative size instead of the heavily distorted Mercator projection. The General Assembly vote was 164-1, with the US casting the only opposing vote.
Friday also marked 25 years since the September 11 attacks on the US. Fyodor Lukyanov argued that the attacks ended America’s post-Cold War sense of security, and its response accelerated the decline of the unipolar order it dominated.

articles.title: Welcome to the post-Western weapons market
articles.body:
Welcome to the post-Western weapons market
The second El Alamein International Airshow took place on September 8-10 at El Alamein International Airport in Egypt. The airshow reaffirmed its status as one of the premier military exhibitions in North Africa and the Middle East. Its international prestige was confirmed by the list of participating nations; the organizers succeeded in bringing together fierce rivals – the leading players in the global defense industry from Russia, the US, China, and Europe.
The airshow’s target audience included defense officials, military commanders, government delegations, and the business elite. Overall, it attracted over 250 exhibitors from 50 countries. More than 12,000 industry professionals visited the stands and displays. The roar of jet engines shook the skies over the Mediterranean Sea as aerobatic teams from Egypt, the UAE, and Türkiye, as well as renowned Russian aerobatic pilots, performed complex maneuvers and showcased their skills. Meanwhile, on the ground, multibillion-dollar contracts were signed.
Why sanctions failed to sideline Russia
Russia’s participation was a distinctive feature and highlight of this year’s airshow. Perhaps the largest and most compelling display was mounted by Russian arms exporter Rosoboronexport (part of the Rostec state corporation). In total, Russia showcased over 500 military-grade products at El Alamein.
The key geopolitical and marketing takeaway from the event was clear: Despite unprecedented sanctions pressure from the West, the Russian defense industry not only maintains its position but also generates huge interest among global players.
Foreign delegations lined up at the Russian exhibit. The reason for this intense interest was pragmatic: Russian weaponry has proven its effectiveness in actual high-tech combat scenarios. The performance characteristics of Western systems are often exaggerated in marketing brochures, while their costs are exorbitantly high; however, Russian equipment has undergone real-world testing against modern reconnaissance, electronic warfare, and air defense systems (including in the zone of Russia’s military operation).
Buyers from around the globe – from the Middle East to Latin America – also appreciate the fact that Moscow offers fair contract terms, free from political blackmail or ideological demands. Historical continuity also plays a major role; many so-called ‘Third World’ countries have traditionally relied on Soviet and Russian weaponry and are familiar with it. Consequently, many of these countries are unwilling to trade reliable Russian equipment for pretty ‘toys’ from other manufacturers.
Combat experience reshapes Russia’s export arsenal
What did Russia showcase at the El Alamein airshow? The star of both the static display and the flying display was the Russian Su-57E fifth-generation multi-role fighter jet. The aerobatic performance by Sukhoi Company chief pilot, Hero of Russia Sergey Bogdan, demonstrated the unsurpassed aerodynamics of modern aviation technology. The aircraft embodies a rich legacy of excellence: Unique aerobatic maneuvers combined with powerful missile and electronic warfare capabilities define the modern Su-57. It carries a new generation of weapon systems – specifically, missiles housed in internal bays. These include air-to-air missiles of various ranges as well as air-to-ground strike systems.
The Yak-130M combat-capable trainer is an upgraded version of the Yak-130 jet trainer. The airshow marked the aircraft’s debut in the Middle East. The Yak-130M is equipped with a full-fledged onboard radar and carries an expanded arsenal of precision-guided weapons, transforming it from a trainer aircraft into a formidable and cost-effective light fighter and attack aircraft. The new model met with immediate success at the airshow; Director General of Rosoboronexport Aleksander Mikheev announced that the first contract for its delivery to a foreign customer was already signed.
But these were not the only examples of Russia’s success at the airshow. State-of-the-art Russian-designed strike munitions were unveiled publicly for the first time at El Alamein. These include the S-71M Monokhrom missile-drone, the S-71K Kover strike drone, and the S8000 Banderol precision-guided drone-missile. The Monokhrom missile-drone comes in a futuristic design with a trapezoidal fuselage cross-section, a folding swept wing, and a V-shaped all-moving tail unit. It is deployed from the internal weapons bays of Su-57 carrier aircraft. The Kover strike drone is the ‘younger brother’ of the Monokhrom – a simpler drone designed for mass deployment from external hardpoints. Its mission is to operate jointly with manned aircraft, exposing and exhausting enemy air defense systems to clear the path for primary missiles, while simultaneously engaging ground targets.
The Banderol precision-guided drone-missile is a next-generation precision-guided stealth munition that has seen extensive use in recent months in Russia’s military operation zone. This drone-missile can be launched from carrier drones and helicopters without the launch platforms entering the enemy’s air defense zone. The combined use of such munitions ensures 100% penetration of any modern air defense system.
Russian defense enterprises also unveiled several new air defense systems. The TKB-1167 four-barrel anti-drone combat module is capable of automatically detecting and engaging UAVs. It made its international debut at the airshow. Additionally, the cutting-edge ZAK-30 Citadel anti-aircraft artillery system with a 30 mm automatic cannon turret was showcased for the first time. The exhibition also featured the Pantsir-SMD-E air defense system, the Verba man-portable air-defense system (MANPADS), and an airspace monitoring system designed to coordinate the use of these systems. Essentially, the Russian defense industry is displaying military equipment developed and shaped by actual combat experience acquired during the Ukraine conflict.
The global arms market moves beyond Western dominance
And what did Russia’s competitors bring to the event? The Egyptian airshow vividly demonstrated the nature of the modern multipolar world. While delegations stormed the Russian pavilions, other major powers sought to draw attention to their own displays.
China mounted an impressive display, underscoring its ambitions on the African continent and its growing military partnership with Cairo. On display were J-16 fighter jets – a mainstay of the PLA Air Force – which are already familiar to Egyptian audiences from recent joint exercises involving Egyptian Rafale fighters. During the flying display, the YY-20 aerial refueling tanker performed a spectacular demonstration of mid-air refueling.
‘Partners’ from across the Atlantic also participated in the Egyptian airshow. The US Air Force displayed proven, serial-production aircraft that Washington is actively promoting in the Middle East market – specifically A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft, which has demonstrated its ability to target slower drones like the Shahed. Playing the role of the “old workhorse that never fails” were 4th-generation multi-role fighters – the F-15E Strike Eagle and F-16 Fighting Falcon – as well as the C-130J/H Hercules military transport aircraft. These aircraft were featured in the static display and attracted certain interest; their primary purpose, however, appeared to be a “show of the flag.”
France and Türkiye demonstrated ambitious aircraft and drone models. As expected, French company Dassault Aviation brought its Rafale fighters. The French strategy was targeted: The exhibition coincided with behind-the-scenes negotiations regarding Egypt’s purchase of an additional batch of 24 such aircraft. Türkiye, represented by the TAI and ASELSAN corporations, played to its strengths by presenting a wide range of strike drones and tactical electronic warfare (EW) systems optimized for the specific conditions of the African theater of operations.
Ultimately, El Alamein International Airshow demonstrated that the rules of the game in the arms market have changed. Attempts to isolate the Russian defense industry have undoubtedly failed. At a time when customers require weapons capable of prevailing in modern high-tech conflicts, Russia’s technological superiority in aviation, air defense, and unmanned systems establishes it as a key and indispensable partner on the international stage.

articles.title: Russia deploys highest number of nuclear warheads in nine years – SIPRI
articles.body:
Russia deploys highest number of nuclear warheads in nine years – SIPRI
Russia has increased the number of nuclear warheads deployed on launchers and ready for use for the fourth consecutive year. The figure has reached its highest level since 2017 amid increasingly frequent nuclear threats by Russian officials against European countries.
Source: The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI)'s 2026 annual report, World Nuclear Forces
Details: According to SIPRI analysts, as of January 2026, Russia's nuclear arsenal consisted of 5,420 warheads. Of these, 2,604 were held in central storage, 1,020 were considered retired and 1,796 warheads were deployed on launchers.
The number of warheads deployed on launchers in Russia has steadily increased since the beginning of the full-scale war against Ukraine. There were 1,588 in 2022, 1,674 in 2023, 1,710 in 2024 and 1,718 in 2025.
Compared with 2020, the Kremlin has increased the number of deployed nuclear warheads by 14%, the highest figure since 2017, when there were 1,950.
By comparison, the US, which has a similarly sized arsenal, has not changed the number of its deployed warheads. The figure remains at 1,770.
France and the UK have also kept their figures unchanged, with 280 and 120 deployed warheads respectively.
China, meanwhile, increased the number of its deployed warheads from 24 to 34, out of a total arsenal of 620.
In 2025, India deployed 12 nuclear warheads on nuclear-powered submarines for the first time. Analysts estimate that New Delhi's total nuclear arsenal stands at 190 warheads.
SIPRI experts noted in its analysis of Russia's nuclear triad that Russia's land-based forces can carry up to 1,092 warheads. At present, around 892 warheads are deployed on intercontinental ballistic missiles.
The Russian Navy has 13 strategic submarines with a combined capacity of 928 warheads. As two submarines are undergoing major refits, the actual number of deployed warheads available to the fleet is 704.
Another 586 warheads are deployed on Russia's strategic bombers. SIPRI analysts noted that in 2025, the Russian Aerospace Forces suffered operational losses following attacks by Ukraine's defence forces on Russian air bases.
This forced the Russian military command to disperse a significant number of Tu-160/M and Tu-95MS aircraft to the remote Belaya air base in Irkutsk Oblast, Dyagilevo air base in Ryazan Oblast and Olenya air base in Murmansk Oblast.
The institute's experts point out that Russia's nuclear modernisation programme is facing significant delays due to Western sanctions, industrial inefficiency and the prioritisation of conventional weapons production for the war in Ukraine. Despite this, Moscow continues to deploy new systems, such as Oreshnik missile systems, including in Belarus.
The report also recorded growing secrecy surrounding nuclear arsenals around the world. This has been influenced by the expiry in February 2026 of the Russian-US Treaty on Measures for the Further Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms (New START), which was not extended.
Quote: "While the global total inventory of nuclear warheads continues to fall as retired weapons are gradually dismantled, year-on-year increases can be seen in the number of operational (stockpiled) nuclear warheads. This trend seems likely to continue and will probably accelerate in the coming years."
Background:
- In November 2024, Russia updated its nuclear doctrine, expanding the list of scenarios in which the use of weapons of mass destruction could be considered.
- In February 2026, the New START Treaty expired. The agreement was not replaced by a new treaty, depriving the international community of an important source of transparency.
- In addition, Russian and Belarusian leaders have repeatedly claimed that tactical nuclear weapons, Iskander systems and Oreshnik missiles have been deployed in Belarus.

articles.title: China’s nuclear stockpile climbs to 620 warheads, SIPRI says
articles.body:
- SIPRI estimates China's nuclear stockpile rose to about 620 warheads by January 2026, up from roughly 600 the year before.
- China displayed new nuclear-capable systems at its September 2025 parade and may have started deploying a small number of warheads with operational forces, though most remain in storage.
China’s nuclear weapon stockpile grew to an estimated 620 warheads as of January 2026, up from about 600 a year earlier, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s newly published World Nuclear Forces assessment. SIPRI researchers Hans M. Kristensen and Matt Korda say the increase is part of a broader expansion that shows no sign of slowing.
The stockpile remains far smaller than those of the United States and Russia, which together hold roughly 86 percent of the world’s nuclear warheads. But China now operates more land-based intercontinental ballistic missile launchers than either country, and SIPRI projects it could match their ICBM numbers by the end of the decade.
Most of China’s arsenal is still kept separate from its launchers, a long-standing peacetime practice meant to prevent accidental or unauthorized use. That may be starting to change. The U.S. Department of Defense has reported that China appears to be mating warheads with missiles in a few mobile battalions during exercises, a departure from the de-mated posture it has maintained for decades. The Pentagon also assessed in 2025 that China had loaded more than 100 missiles into three newly built silo fields, though there is no public evidence those missiles carry live warheads. U.S. officials have separately told SIPRI’s authors, on condition of anonymity, that a Chinese ballistic missile submarine on deterrence patrol may be carrying nuclear-armed missiles.
Based on these assessments, SIPRI estimates China may have deployed a small number of warheads with operational forces, perhaps as many as 34, as of January 2026. The vast majority of the arsenal remains in central and regional storage.
China put several previously unseen nuclear-capable systems on display at its September 2025 Victory Day parade in Beijing. These included a silo-loading vehicle for the DF-31B intercontinental ballistic missile and a new DF-61 ICBM launcher that SIPRI says closely resembles the existing DF-41. The parade also featured JL-3 submarine-launched ballistic missiles, which China has fitted to upgraded Type 094A ballistic missile submarines, and a JL-1 air-launched ballistic missile shown publicly for the first time.
“China’s early warning infrared satellites can reportedly detect an incoming ICBM within 90 seconds of launch with an early warning alert sent to a command center within three to four minutes,” the Pentagon said in its 2025 report on Chinese military power, as cited by SIPRI.
That capability points to what the U.S. Department of Defense calls an “early warning counterstrike” strategy, a launch posture similar to those long used by Russia and the United States. SIPRI notes the approach would let Beijing fire a retaliatory strike before an incoming attack detonates, provided the warning data can be confirmed through a second, independent detection method.
Despite the shift toward faster reaction times, China has continued to publicly affirm its no-first-use policy, most recently in a white paper on arms control released in November 2025. Beijing has held that position since testing its first nuclear device in 1964.
China is also working on a next-generation Type 096 submarine to eventually replace its current Jin-class boats, though SIPRI says that program appears to be running behind schedule. On the delivery side, the country is developing a new strategic bomber intended to carry the JL-1 missile shown at the parade, and it increased the number of dual-capable DF-26 intermediate-range missile launchers in its inventory during 2025 while also fielding a conventional anti-ship variant of the same missile.
China has had the technical means to fit multiple warheads on a single missile since the early 1980s but did not do so until 2014, when it added multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles to the DF-5B. It extended that capability to the DF-41 in 2020. SIPRI notes that China appears not to have deployed MIRVs as widely as its technology would allow, including on the missiles loaded into its new silo fields.
SIPRI’s tables list China’s stockpile as split across roughly 20 nuclear-capable H-6N bombers, land-based missile forces with 775 launchers carrying an estimated 509 warheads, and 72 submarine-launched missiles carrying 72 warheads, with about 19 additional warheads believed to be in reserve for systems approaching operational status. The institute cautions that its estimates of Chinese deployment levels carry considerable uncertainty, given Beijing’s limited public disclosure of its nuclear forces.

Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) dismantled Russia’s RM-48U ballistic missile and revealed that the weapon was assembled from repurposed S-300 and S-400 missile components.
Intelligence analysts discovered that the missile relied heavily on foreign electronics, including dozens of parts manufactured by companies based in the United States.
