articles.title: Iran obtained Chinese satellite images before deadly strike on US troops, officials say
articles.body:
Iran obtained high-resolution satellite imagery from Chinese sources before carrying out a missile attack on a U.S. air base in Jordan that killed three American soldiers, U.S. officials familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal.
The officials described the finding as the clearest evidence to date that Chinese support for Iran has had lethal consequences for U.S. forces.
They said Washington had linked the imagery to the July 17 attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in northeastern Jordan, where Iranian ballistic missiles struck a residential compound housing U.S. troops.
Three American soldiers were killed and four others wounded. U.S. officials also told the Journal that Iran targeted manned and unmanned aircraft stationed at the base.
The officials did not identify the Chinese entities that supplied the imagery and did not accuse the Chinese government of direct involvement. Iran obtained satellite images both before and after the attack, they said.
The disclosure threatens to add another source of tension between Washington and Beijing less than two weeks before Chinese leader Xi Jinping is due to meet President Donald Trump at the White House on September 24.
U.S. officials have grown increasingly frustrated over what they describe as Beijing's refusal to address repeated warnings that Chinese companies have been supplying Iran with satellite imagery that could be used to target American personnel and military assets in the Middle East.
Senior U.S. officials raised the satellite imagery linked to the July 17 attack directly with Chinese counterparts, according to the Journal, but Beijing rejected the allegations and demanded evidence.
Chinese officials have repeatedly dismissed Washington's concerns and refused to acknowledge that Chinese companies were engaged in such activity, the report said.
China's Foreign Ministry accused "certain parties" of attempting to drag Beijing into the conflict. The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not respond to the Journal's request for comment.
A strike that exposed a growing threat
The attack on Muwaffaq Salti was one of three separate missile strikes on the base within 24 hours and represented a significant escalation in the conflict.
The deaths were the first U.S. military fatalities since the April ceasefire and underscored the difficulty of protecting American personnel even at a heavily defended installation.
They also intensified concerns in Washington over Iran's improving ability to accurately strike U.S. targets.
Trump administration officials had spent months warning their Chinese counterparts that Chinese companies were providing satellite imagery Iran could potentially use to target American forces and assets in the region.
In May, the administration imposed sanctions on several Chinese companies, saying their provision of satellite imagery to Iran "poses a threat to U.S. and allied personnel."
Within three days of the July attack, Iran released high-resolution images showing damage in three separate sections of the Jordanian base.
The Wall Street Journal said its analysis of lower-resolution satellite imagery available to the public showed damage to more than 20 structures across those three areas.
Analysts and former officials cautioned that imagery from Chinese sources was likely only one part of the intelligence picture available to Tehran.
Iran's military also relies on its own satellites and human intelligence networks, while receiving intelligence and imagery from Russia, U.S. officials cited by the Journal said.
Trump seeks to avoid clash with Beijing
The revelations come at a particularly sensitive moment in U.S.-China relations.
Trump has told his team that maintaining a good relationship with China, and with Xi personally, is a top priority, according to the Journal.
U.S. officials have consequently sought to avoid public confrontations with Beijing that could overshadow or disrupt preparations for the September 24 summit.
A White House official told the newspaper that no outside assistance received by Iran had meaningfully improved its ability to attack the United States, without directly addressing the findings concerning the satellite imagery.
Senior administration officials have also publicly played down the significance of any Chinese assistance to Tehran.
Days after the July 17 attack, Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi.
Asked afterward whether China was supplying Iran with intelligence for targeting purposes, Rubio declined to answer directly, saying that "nothing China did altered in any way the course of the conflict."
The dispute nevertheless adds a new security dimension to the Trump-Xi meeting, as Washington weighs its desire to preserve ties with Beijing against mounting concerns that Chinese technology and commercial services may be strengthening Iran's ability to identify and strike American targets in the Middle East.

articles.title: As Russia targets gas stations, Kyiv draws up plans for possible fuel shortages, Klitschko says
articles.body:
As Russia targets gas stations, Kyiv draws up plans for possible fuel shortages, Klitschko says
Kyiv authorities don't have the resources to build shelters at every gas station, while the city also faces a shortage of weapons needed to intercept Russian drones and missiles, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Sept. 11.
Klitschko's remarks come as Moscow has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine's capital, including at least four strikes on gas stations over the past week. Kyiv has faced near non-stop drone attacks in recent days, killing and injuring civilians.
According to the mayor, protecting gas stations from Russian attacks is a "complicated issue."
"The issue of protection is a question of air defense. Speaking with the military, I can say that, unfortunately, we have a shortage of means of destruction — those missiles that work against drones, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles. There is a problem with this," Klitschko told reporters on the sidelines of the Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference.
The Sept. 10 attack marked the first time Russian troops targeted a gas station in Kyiv, after similar attacks had largely been concentrated in frontline areas. The expanding campaign is disrupting fuel distribution, potentially affecting both civilians and military personnel who rely on passenger vehicles.
Klitschko said authorities have stockpiled fuel for the winter and in case of emergencies. The reserves will help keep generators running during possible power outages, he added, as many expect Russia to again seek to cripple Ukraine's energy grid ahead of winter.
"We are working through various plans," Klitschko said. "We must be prepared for different scenarios, including a bad one."

articles.title: Russian Strikes Kill 2 In Zaporizhzhia, Wound At Least 17 In Odesa
articles.body:
A fresh round of Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least three people and wounded dozens of others over the past 24 hours, Ukraine's president said on September 12, adding that the strikes targeted civilian sites and infrastructure across the country.
"Since the night, there have been virtually constant strikes on our cities and communities," Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media. "Ten regions were under Russian strikes last night, and Russian attack drones are still flying in many of them."
Two people were killed and six others were wounded by a Shahed-type drone strike on residential buildings in the Zaporizhzhia region, he said, adding that a missile attack on "critical infrastructure" in Kryviy Rih killed one person and injured three others.
In Odesa, 37 people were injured when a high-rise residential building was hit by Russian missile overnight, and rescue operations were under way at the site. The search continued for two people that were unaccounted for, Zelenskyy said.
Earlier, local officials in Odesa said that a 25-story residential building had been damaged, with apartments on the 21st through 23rd floors catching fire. The upper floors were destroyed.
Three other residential buildings were also damaged in Odesa, officials said.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia attacked the country with ballistic and cruise missiles and 129 attack drones, including jet-powered Shahed-type drones. It said Ukrainian air defenses had destroyed or suppressed 110 of the targets.
The air force said strikes were recorded in 20 locations across the country and falling debris in four others. It said the Odesa region was the most affected.
The attacks came a day after Russian strikes killed at least six people in Zaporizhzhia and other parts of Ukraine, as Moscow and Kyiv have traded strikes on logistics, energy, and other economic infrastructure in recent weeks.
Russia's Defense Ministry claimed on September 12 that Russian forces had hit the Zaporizhstal steel plant in Zaporizhzhia, as well as an Interpipe Steel complex in Dnipro and several facilities in Kryviy Rih, including the Northern Iron Ore Beneficiation Works complex.
The ministry also said its forces had struck two cargo vessels overnight in the Ukrainian Black Sea port of Chornomorsk, according to Russia's Interfax news agency.
The claims cannot be independently verified.
The attacks followed a deadly Russian assault on Zaporizhzhia on September 11, when one person was killed, according to Ukrainian officials. Russia also struck other parts of Ukraine that day, including Kyiv, where attacks on two petrol stations killed two people and wounded at least 12.
Russia has intensified its air campaign against Ukraine in recent weeks, including repeated attacks with faster jet-powered drones. The strikes have increasingly hit logistics and economic targets as fighting along the front line has largely stalled.
On September 10, Russian strikes killed five people in the southeastern industrial city of Pavlohrad and also hit a petrol station in Kyiv and a sunflower-oil facility operated by US-based Bunge in Dnipro.
Ukraine Strikes Economic, Industrial Targets
Ukraine has also stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russian economic and industrial targets.
On September 12, Ukrainian drones struck industrial facilities in Russia's Samara region, Interfax reported, citing regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev. He did not specify which facilities were targeted or the extent of the damage.
Ukraine's military said it had struck the Togliattikauchuk plant, one of Russia's largest producers of synthetic rubber, in the city of Togliatti, causing a fire.
The Ukrainian General Staff said the plant produces synthetic rubber and fuel additives used in fuel for Russian missiles. The claim could not be independently verified.
The mayor of Togliatti said several residential buildings were damaged and one person was injured.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it had downed 230 Ukrainian drones overnight over more than a dozen Russian regions, as well as over Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014.
In a separate attack, four commercial properties were set ablaze in the southern Russian city of Taganrog, local officials said.

articles.body:
Modi and Xi seek to reset India-China ties on BRICS sidelines
The two leaders ‘expressed commitment’ to resolving contested border issue, India’s foreign ministry said.
The leaders of India and China have agreed to work together towards resolving the contested border issue, according to the foreign ministry in New Delhi.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping met on Saturday on the sidelines of the summit of the BRICS group of emerging nations in New Delhi.

- list 4 of 4Putin, Pezeshkian in India for BRICS summit clouded by Iran and Ukraine war
It is Xi’s first trip to India in seven years and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals is being closely watched.
“Although our two countries are different in many respects, they are fully capable of complementing each other’s strengths, supporting one another, achieving mutual success and advancing together,” Xi said in a video released from New Delhi as he met Modi.
After the meeting, India’s foreign ministry said “the two leaders expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question”.
Modi “underlined the need for both sides to observe existing agreements and understandings on border related issues,” the statement added.
They pledged to build up their countries’ cultural, business and transport links, New Delhi said.
“On economic and trade relations, they underlined the need to address each other’s concerns, including structural trade imbalance and supply chain issues, and facilitation of meaningful and predictable market access,” it added.
Areas for cooperation growing
Xi said Beijing has always viewed and developed China-India relations from a strategic and long-term perspective, reported the state-run Xinhua news agency.
Institutional exchanges between the two countries are gradually being restored, the list of areas for cooperation is growing and bilateral trade has reached a new high, Xi said, according to Xinhua.
Xi landed in New Delhi earlier on Saturday with his entourage, including Foreign Minister, Wang Yi, and high-ranking Chinese Communist Party official, Cai Qi.
The trip comes six years after the deadly military clash along India and China’s disputed border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
The underlying territorial dispute in the Tibet region remains unresolved and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500km (2,175 mile) high-altitude border.
“They are looking for ‘early and substantial harvest’ when it comes to the border issue,” Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne, said, as reported by the AFP news agency. “You cannot have a buildup of your forces on the border … but at the same time say ‘we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships.'”
Deep mistrust remains, however, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
Dozens of Tibetans living in exile, including their spiritual leader the Dalai Lama, protested in New Delhi on Friday, waving placards against Xi’s visit.
BRICS leaders gather
The Russian and Iranian presidents were among the leaders who arrived in the Indian capital on Friday for the BRICS summit.
On Saturday, the 11-nation bloc issued a joint declaration calling for calm in the Middle East and stressing the need to work together to maintain the smooth flow of global trade.
The conflicts in Palestine, Iran and Ukraine, along with global trade turbulence and energy security, were expected to dominate the two-day meeting.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin held talks with Modi on Friday and agreed to further strengthen the “special” relationship between their countries.
During a meeting with Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian, Modi underscored the need to protect freedom of navigation and commerce, as well as the safety and wellbeing of ships’ crews.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the United States-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.

articles.title: BRICS New Delhi declaration rejects sanctions, nuclear threats and terrorism
articles.body:
BRICS New Delhi declaration rejects sanctions, nuclear threats and terrorism
The BRICS nations on Saturday called out “unilateral coercive measures,” condemned terrorism, and called for the peaceful resolution of global disputes through dialogue and diplomacy in their summit declaration.
The declaration adopted by the BRICS leaders at their 18th summit in New Delhi reaffirmed the bloc’s “opposition to unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law” and the UN charter, and called to eliminate them.
The leaders of emerging and developing countries pointed out that sanctions and secondary sanctions have “far-reaching negative implications” including for human rights and food security, and disproportionately affect the poor and vulnerable.
The BRICS leaders repeated their earlier calls to reform the UN and other global institutions to reflect the new global realities. The New Delhi declaration stressed that no single country or group of countries should have a monopoly over senior positions in the UN – which was formed in the aftermath of World War 2.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi made the same point while addressing the leaders, saying a “rapidly changing world can no longer be governed by outdated institutions.”

— RT_India (@RT_India_news) September 12, 2026
Importantly, China and Russia, the two BRICS members who are also permanent members of the Security Council, reiterated their support for “Brazil and India to play a greater role in the UN, including its Security Council.”
BRICS, which started as a five-member grouping two decades ago, has now expanded to 11 full members, raising its economic size and global influence.
The adoption of the 45-page declaration is itself seen as a success for Indian diplomacy, which was able to unite Iran and the United Arab Emirates – on different sides of the Middle East conflict – behind the document.
The presence of Chinese President Xi Jinping in New Delhi – after seven years – along with Russian President Vladimir Putin, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has added to the gathering’s gravitas amid rising global tensions and economic turbulence.
The BRICS leaders condemned all acts of terrorism as “criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation” – a point that host India has repeatedly made at various global fora. The declaration specifically condemned the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir in April last year, in which 26 civilians were killed. India clashed with nuclear-armed neighbor Pakistan with drones and missiles following that attack.
The BRICS countries also called out the unilateral blockade of Cuba, and expressed concern over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities in violation of resolutions by the International Atomic Energy Agency.
While the document does not mention the Ukraine conflict, it says ”nuclear safeguards, safety, and security must always be upheld, including in armed conflicts, to protect people and the environment from harm” – an obvious reference to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant, which has seen attacks by Ukrainian forces endangering its safety.
The BRICS nations opposed the forced displacement of the Palestinian people from “Occupied Palestinian Territory,” and any geographic or demographic changes in the Gaza Strip. They further called on Israel to withdraw its forces from all Lebanese territories.
The next BRICS summit will be held in China.

articles.title: Russia offers war-tested drones and missiles for export – expert
articles.body:
Russia offers war-tested drones and missiles for export – expert
Can Kasapoglu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, said this in an analytical review on the situation in the Russian-Ukrainian war.
"Russia is converting its industrial and operational experience gained in Ukraine – including mass-produced affordable munitions, cruise-missile-drone hybrids, and saturation attacks using mixed strike packages – into an increasingly competitive defense-export portfolio," the expert said.
Russia presented some of its export products at the El Alamein International Airshow 2026, held in Egypt on September 8-10.
"Russia dispatched its combat-tested drones and missiles to Egypt to promote them for export," Kasapoglu said.
One example is the export version of the Banderol cruise-missile-drone hybrid. Russia displayed the Dan-T loitering munition. A derivative of the Banderol missile, the turbojet-powered Dan-T weighs up to 272 kg, has a range of approximately 450 km, and can be launched from fixed-wing drones or rotary-wing manned aircraft – primarily Mi-28 variants. Kronstadt JSC, the manufacturer of the Orion reconnaissance-strike drone, produces Banderol.
Russia began testing the system in secret in 2024. Its first documented use against Ukraine came in spring 2025, when Ukrainian intelligence reconstructed the hybrid from debris.
According to the expert, Banderol resembles a scaled-down Kh-101, with deployable wings and radar-signature-reducing shaping.
The expert points out that Banderol's architecture combines a Chinese Swiwin turbojet and inertial-navigation system, American, European, and Japanese electronics, and Russia's Kometa-8 controlled radiation pattern antenna. It costs an estimated $50,000-$150,000, compared with roughly $2 million for the Kh-101 and $1.5 million for the Iskander-K. It reaches some 595 km/h per hour, travels 500 km, and carries a 113-kg high-explosive fragmentation warhead
"The Ukrainian military is trying to find interception weapons to counter the Banderol, including products from the Shahed-hunter Wild Hornets drone technology group," Kasapoglu wrote.
The expert also noted that the Russian defense industry sent an export version of the Lancet drone, the Lancet-E, to Egypt. The system has warhead variants weighing approximately 2.7 kg and 4.5 kg. The basic version of the Lancet has an operational range of about 40 km and contains a significant number of Western-made components.
In July, Russia planned to produce 120 Bandеrol missiles per month, but the plant had not yet reached its target production rate. In August, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate reported that Russia was capable of producing up to 80 Bandеrol missiles per month.

articles.title: Saudi pipeline attack exposes growing power of Iran-backed militias - analysis
articles.body:
Iranian-backed militias in Iraq were responsible for an attack on a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia. The Iraqi government confirmed on Saturday that the attack came from Iraq’s Maysan province. A local commander has been dismissed, the Rudaw media channel in Iraq said. Iraq has sought to prevent Saudi Arabia from retaliating by admitting the attack came from Iraq.
The attack on Saudi Arabia shows how the militias threaten the region. By cutting off energy trade, the militias are also threatening the world. The militias, such as Kataib Hezbollah, have attacked Saudi Arabia in the past. They also killed three American service members in Jordan in 2024. As part of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of militias, they have not only attacked Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Syria, but also Israel and likely several other Gulf states. Iran’s proxy militias in Iraq are growing in their threats.
The militias in Iraq were supposed to be reined in by the new Iraqi prime minister Ali al Zaidi. He had vowed that they would either be disarmed or have their arms put under state control. However, the militias are trying to play for time. They know that US forces are leaving Iraq by September 30. US air defenses are also reported to be moving out of key areas such as the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq. This enables the militias to fill the vacuum in some areas, increasing their potential threats and control.
US, Saudi Arabia strike Iraqi militias
Back in July, the US and Saudi Arabia carried out strikes on the militias after similar attacks on Saudi Arabia. US Central Command said at the time on July 28 that “US Central Command and the Saudi Arabian Armed Forces conducted precision strikes in Iraq, July 28, against Iran-aligned terrorists that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) directed to attack US forces and Saudi energy infrastructure.”
CENCOM said in July that “US and Saudi fighter aircraft struck multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq in a strong response to over 30 IRGC-directed aerial drone attacks in the last 72 hours. The unwarranted attacks against US forces were not successful. From February through April 2026, there were more than 600 attempted attacks on US citizens and facilities by Iran-aligned terrorist militias in Iraq.”
The attacks have not stopped. In fact, it appears the militias are working closely with Iran’s IRGC and the Houthis to spread havoc. The attack on the pipeline came as the Houthis also seized islands in Yemen that enable them to threaten the Bab al Mandeb Strait.
Rudaw media said “Iraq has previously denied Saudi claims that attacks on the kingdom's energy infrastructure originated from Iraqi territory, making Saturday's confirmation a rare acknowledgment by Baghdad that its territory was used as a launchpad for an attack on a neighboring country.” Now Iraq’s prime minister has "directed the formation of an investigative board concerning the Maysan Operations Command.”
Rudaw noted that Zaidi also "ordered that the Operations Commander be relieved of his position, following confirmation that the attacks targeting our brothers in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia were launched from a location within the province.” Rudaw added that “the announcement came shortly after Saudi Arabia said drones launched from Iraq had struck its East-West oil pipeline, causing casualties and damage. Baghdad condemned the attack and announced an urgent investigation to identify those responsible.”
Riyadh faces threats from multiple fronts
Iraq has asked Saudi Arabia not to respond. Riyadh has a problem in that it now faces threats from multiple fronts. The Houthis have also attacked Saudi Arabia. Riyadh faces threats from Iraq and Yemen. Riyadh has been in touch with the US. It has also received some verbal support from its Mecca Pact allies, Pakistan and Turkey. However, military support is lacking. US President Donald Trump has also mentioned the Houthis but appeared to make it seem that they have been in touch with the White House and are trying to de-escalate.
According to Arab News in Saudi Arabia, “Saudi Arabia temporarily shut down its East-West Pipeline after it was targeted in several drone attacks in the Riyadh and Madinah regions, the Ministry of Energy said on Friday.” It said several people were injured. “Emergency and specialized technical teams were deployed immediately following the attacks to secure the pipeline and assess its safety in coordination with the relevant authorities, the ministry added.”
The Kingdom will “give the brotherly Iraqi government an opportunity to take the necessary measures to prevent attacks launched from Iraqi territory against the Kingdom and neighboring countries,” the ministry said. Saudi Arabia appears to be giving Iraq time to show it can deal with the culprits. Riyadh is also taking a wait and see approach on Yemen.
Iraqi militias, a growing threat to the region
The attacks by the militias in Iraq illustrate how they are a growing threat to the region and the world. The world, because the energy issues in the region affect the world. Iranian-backed militias have become one of the most powerful groups in Iraq since the fall of Saddam Hussein in 2003. Many trace their origins to earlier organizations created during the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s, when groups such as the Badr Organization were established with support from Iran's IRGC.
After 2003, Iran expanded its influence by supporting additional militias, including Kata'ib Hezbollah, Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba, Kata'ib Sayyid al-Shuhada, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, and Kata'ib al-Imam Ali. Many of these groups later became part of the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), which were formally established in 2014 to help fight ISIS after the collapse of Iraqi army units in northern Iraq. While the PMF played an important role in defeating ISIS, several factions retained close ties to Tehran and continued to operate independently of the Iraqi state. Many of the militias are sanctioned by the US as terrorist groups.
Today, Iraq's effort to place all weapons under state control has exposed divisions within the PMF. Several factions have agreed in principle to integrate fully into the state's security structure, while five prominent Iran-aligned groups continue to resist. These include Kata'ib Hezbollah, Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba, Kata'ib Sayyid al-Shuhada, Ansar Allah al-Awfiya, and Saraya Awliya al-Dam.
These groups argue that they should not disarm until all foreign forces leave Iraq and the country achieves what they describe as full sovereignty. Baghdad, backed by Washington, maintains that a state monopoly on arms is essential for Iraq's stability, sovereignty, and economic development. The debate over these militias has therefore become one of the defining security and political issues facing Iraq today.
What’s important to know is that the militias continue to grow their power and show they can threaten neighboring states using the pinpoint accuracy of drones and other weapons. This illustrates their growing threat.

articles.title: At least 11 killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine as Kyiv strikes Russia's 'shadow fleet'
articles.body:
The strikes hit several regions, with Odesa suffering particularly badly. At the same time, Kyiv is pursuing an operation against Russia's "shadow fleet", aiming to choke off a key source of war funding
At least 11 people were killed and 96 injured across Ukraine in overnight Russian attacks between 11 and 12 September.
The Odesa region was hit hardest, but strikes also targeted, among others, the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kyiv, Sumy, Kharkiv and Kherson regions.
According to Ukraine's Air Force, Russia used 129 drones of various types, as well as Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, eight Kalibr cruise missiles and six guided Kh-59/69 missiles. Around half of the drones deployed were fitted with jet engines.
Ukraine's air defences destroyed or disrupted 110 aerial targets, including six Kalibr missiles, two Kh-59/69 missiles, one S-8000 Banderol cruise missile launched from a drone and 101 unmanned aerial vehicles.
Attack on Odesa
One of the main targets of the overnight attack was Odesa. At around 5.30 a.m., Ukraine's Air Force warned that Russian cruise missiles were heading towards the city from over the Black Sea.
A multi-storey residential building was damaged in the strike. "The enemy attacked the city. A multi-storey residential building has been damaged," said Odesa region governor Oleh Kiper.
The number of wounded in the Odesa region rose as more information came in about the aftermath of the attack. In the end, at least 35 people were injured, including a five-month-old baby and a 17-year-old. Some of the victims required hospitalisation.
Russian attacks in the Dnipropetrovsk region
Russian forces also attacked the Dnipropetrovsk region. In Dnipro, drones, artillery and air-dropped bombs damaged an industrial facility, residential buildings, garages and vehicles. One person was killed and 19 were injured.
During the night another Russian strike hit an industrial plant in Kryvyi Rih. One person was killed and three were wounded. A 54-year-old man was taken to hospital in a serious condition.
In total, two people were killed and at least 22 wounded in the Dnipropetrovsk region, including a child, governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
Russian attacks also hit the Zaporizhzhia region. Over the past 24 hours, Russian forces have carried out strikes on 45 towns and villages, including five missile attacks on Zaporizhzhia city. Two people were killed and 11 injured in the region.
In the Donetsk region, four people were killed and five wounded. Two people died in Sloviansk, one in Kramatorsk and another in Yasnohirka, governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In the Kyiv region, one person was killed and three were injured, including a child. Russian attack drones struck five districts: Brovary, Obukhiv, Bucha, Boryspil and Vyshhorod. Fifteen facilities were damaged, including seven houses, vehicles, warehouses, hangars and a power line.
In the Sumy region, a 68-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone strike on the Myropillia community. In a separate attack on the Novoslobidske community, a 64-year-old man was wounded. Over the course of the day, Russian forces carried out more than 50 attacks on 25 localities there, using artillery, mortars, FPV drones, other unmanned aerial vehicles and guided air-dropped bombs.
In the Kharkiv region, a 32-year-old man was killed in an attack on Kharkiv, and a 19-year-old man was wounded elsewhere in the region. Russian forces struck Kharkiv and seven other localities, using guided air-dropped bombs and various types of drones.
In the Kherson region, 18 people were wounded. Russian attacks targeted residential areas as well as critical and social infrastructure. Fifteen residential buildings were damaged, along with shops, a petrol station, a service station, an ambulance and vehicles.
Attack on Russian plant
Ukraine's defence forces confirmed that during the night of 11 to 12 September they carried out a strike on the Tolyattikauchuk plant in Russia's Samara region. The factory supplies products used by the Russian military-industrial complex.
The attack sparked a fire on the plant's premises. "The scale of the damage is still being assessed," Ukraine's General Staff said.
The plant produces, among other things, synthetic rubber, monomers, fractions and additives for high-octane fuels. The Ukrainian military stresses that synthetic rubber is used, among other purposes, in the production of solid fuel for short-range missiles and ballistic rockets.
Earlier, "Ukrainska Pravda" reported a strike by Ukrainian forces on the Machine-Building Plant in Snizhne, located in Russian-occupied territory of the Donetsk region. The plant manufactures components for gas turbine engines, including compressor and turbine discs and blades.
Ukraine targets Russia's "shadow fleet"
As Russia was carrying out its overnight bombardment of Ukraine, Ukrainian forces continued operations aimed at the country's economic backbone.
On 12 September, Robert "Brovdi" Browdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, announced further attacks on Russia's so-called "shadow fleet", used to transport Russian oil in circumvention of some sanctions.
According to Browdi, since the operation began around ten weeks earlier, Ukrainian forces have attacked a total of 285 vessels belonging to Russia's "shadow fleet" operating in the Azov and Black Seas.
The highest number of attacks was recorded in July: 215. In August, a further 54 vessels were struck, and between 1 and 11 September another 16.
Browdi claims that the Ukrainian strikes have almost brought traffic by Russia's "shadow fleet" in the Sea of Azov and the Kerch Strait to a halt. He says the operation has also seriously impeded its activity in the northern and north-eastern parts of the Black Sea.
The commander released footage which, he said, shows an attack by Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces on a sanctioned Russian tanker belonging to the "shadow fleet". The ship was reportedly being escorted by a Russian helicopter.
Browdi stressed that revenues from Russian oil exports are one of the sources of funding for the war against Ukraine. Attacks on vessels involved in transporting Russian oil are therefore intended as part of broader efforts to limit Moscow's financial capabilities.

articles.title: EU Authorized Ukraine to Spend 6.1 Billion Euros on PAC-3 Missiles and Drones
articles.body:
The European Commission has finalized the approval of exemptions from defense procurement rules as part of a €6.1 billion package for Ukraine.
This was announced by European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius, according to European Pravda.
This funding is part of the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan (UASL). Of that amount, €60 billion is earmarked for Ukraine’s defense needs during 2026–2027.
“Today, the Commission officially approved the allocation of 6.1 billion for drones and missiles for Ukraine’s air defense as part of the Ukraine Support Loan,” Kubilius said.
He noted that this decision officially allows Ukraine to procure PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems. They can be ordered, in particular, through the PURL mechanism.
“The package, funded as part of the loans to support Ukraine, includes five waivers from standard rules. Three are for Ukrainian-manufactured drones and components that exceed cost thresholds, and two are for U.S.-manufactured equipment, specifically PAC-3 missiles,” the European Commissioner said.
Kubilius noted that all €28.3 billion allocated for this year to finance Ukraine’s defense through the loan have already been approved.
The European Commission announced on August 24 the approval of a €6.1 billion defense procurement package for Ukraine.
The statement noted that the procurements include the supply of air defense and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition, and radars.
The EU attributes the need to strengthen Ukraine’s air defense to Russia’s increasing use of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that the European Commission had allocated €3.47 billion to Ukraine for the purchase of drones, missiles, air defense systems, and Swedish-made Gripen E fighter jets.

articles.title: BRICS nations urge 'maximum restraint' in Middle East war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
BRICS nations urge 'maximum restraint' in Middle East war
Members of the 11-nation BRICS group including China, Russia, Iran and India called for calm in the Middle East at a summit in New Delhi on Saturday, overcoming earlier divisions to issue a joint statement.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, who joined Russian, Iranian, Indian and other leaders in the Indian capital, told the summit that the war in the Middle East "does not serve the common interests of the international community".
Foreign ministers of the BRICS grouping failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May, with Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on 28 February.
But leaders issued a statement on Saturday after intense diplomatic efforts by host India, as the bloc seeks to bolster its global influence and address conflict, trade turbulence and energy security.
"We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia," the joint statement said, adding the countries "call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation".
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
"We have to transform this pyramid of privilege into a platform of partnership," Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other leaders.
Modi, opening the two-day summit, called for a system "where every country has a voice, every member has a stake and humanity's development is at the centre of every effort".
He told leaders that BRICS nations "represent 50 percent of the world's population, 40 percent of global GDP and more than 25 percent of global trade".
But finding balance in the bloc is a tough diplomatic task.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
Iran's Pezeshkian attended the summit shortly after warning that the Middle East does not need the United States to be a "regional policeman", with the two countries at war and tensions threatening the vital Strait of Hormuz.
Pezeshkian met with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed on the summit sidelines.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow's war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
Modi embraced Putin before talks on Friday. Putin, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.
'Handling differences'
But the summit's other major focus is China.
Xi's visit is also being closely watched because it is his first to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
Xi was given a red-carpet welcome, with an honour guard of soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses, and greeted with a handshake by Modi at the summit venue.
Xi and Modi later met, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported, without providing further details.
His visit comes six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Tibetan border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
Beijing said ahead of his visit that it was "ready to work with India... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences".
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre (2,175-mile) high-altitude border with Tibet.
"They are looking for 'early and substantial harvest' when it comes to the border issue," said Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne.
"You cannot have a build-up of your forces on the border... but at the same time say 'we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships'."
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry continuing to complicate ties.
Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday - exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 - waving placards against Xi's visit.

articles.title: From Russian classrooms to Iran’s defense industry: how Moscow trains Iranian specialists
articles.body:
RFE/RL's investigative project Sistema examined hundreds of Russian-Iranian scientific papers published over the past decade and identified links between Russian universities and Iran's defense industry.
Russia has been invading Ukraine since 2014 and has pounded its cities nightly since 2022 with Shaheds, the Iranian-designed attack drones it turns out by the thousand. And now Russian universities are where some of Iran's military engineers learn their trade, before returning to institutions tied to Iran's army and Revolutionary Guards.
At St Petersburg's ITMO University, Iranian co-authored papers almost equaled German ones in number in 2025, although Germany had been a key partner before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Sistema's count shows.
Academic ties with a military edge
For almost four decades, Russia has trained Iranian engineers in fields including aircraft manufacturing, missile development, satellite navigation, and nuclear technology, Sistema reported. Almost 10,000 Iranian students were enrolled at Russian universities in 2025, 42% more than two years earlier, according to Russia's science ministry. Medicine remains the most popular field.
In some cases, the training goes beyond ordinary academic exchange. In 2018, Iranian students from the Moscow Aviation Institute (MAI) interned at Vympel, a Russian manufacturer of missile weapons, alongside other foreign students, Sistema reported.
The investigation also examined the career of Ali Mohammad Amoui, who completed postgraduate study in gas turbine engines in 2000 at the MATI technological university in Moscow, later absorbed into MAI. From 2017 to 2022, he served as deputy director general for trade and international relations of Farsco Aviation MRO Center, whose shareholders, according to Iranian corporate records cited by the investigation, include Iran's Aviation Industries Organization, part of the country's Defense Ministry, and the sanctioned airline Mahan Air. Farsco presents itself as a civilian maintenance business.
Amoui co-authored research with MAI scientists on protective coatings for turbine blades and the strengthening of titanium components in aircraft engines. He also listed Iran's Malek Ashtar University of Technology, which answers to the Iranian Defense Ministry, as his workplace.
Another area of cooperation is satellite navigation and electronic warfare. Iranian professor Mohammad-Reza Mousavi, who edits a journal published by Iran's naval academy, researched GPS spoofing and worked with specialists at Samara University in 2016.
His PhD student Amir Tabatabaei also studied in Samara and worked on GLONASS, Sistema reported. It added that the two developed a method to detect fake GPS signals and published their research in a journal of the Russian defense concern Elektropribor, which develops navigation systems for the Russian Navy.
Russia and Iran share scientific interests in nuclear physics
Some of this work is dual-use, with civilian and military applications alike. Sistema describes Iranian Mohammad Hosseinpour Khanmiri, who studied methods for measuring uranium and thorium isotopes at St Petersburg State University. By 2022, he had applied a method he had developed with a Russian scientist to ore from Iran’s Saghand deposit. He later listed the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran as his workplace.
His co-authors also had links to Iran’s nuclear program, the investigation reports. Mohammad Outokesh, who studied the operation of gas centrifuges, co-authored a paper with Javad Karimi-Sabet, a deputy head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran. Iran's then president, Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, commended Karimi-Sabet in 2006 for his work on nuclear equipment at Natanz, including a new generation of centrifuges. The US and European countries later imposed sanctions on Karimi-Sabet.

articles.title: Former Russian president threatens to wipe Lithuania "off the map" and says NATO will not defend it
articles.body:
Former Russian president threatens to wipe Lithuania "off the map" and says NATO will not defend it
Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev has claimed that Russia would wipe Lithuania "off the map" if nuclear weapons were deployed on its territory and that its NATO allies would not dare invoke Article 5 on collective defence.
Source: Medvedev during a visit to Russia's Northwestern Federal District, which borders Lithuania, as quoted by Russian propaganda media outlets
Details: Medvedev was responding to a constitutional initiative in Vilnius aimed at repealing a provision that bans the deployment of nuclear weapons on Lithuanian territory.
"They are doing this in vain," he said.
He also threatened a military response if nuclear weapons were deployed in the Baltic country.
"No one will come to their defence. Even if the place is reduced to scorched earth, no other country will go to war for them. And the well-known Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty – it will not be invoked, everyone recognises that. Because if it is invoked, it will be a global catastrophe, a planetary one. They are not fools. But Lithuania will disappear from the map," Medvedev said, once again resorting to apocalyptic threats.
Background:
- In June 2026, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Vilnius was negotiating with the US over the possible deployment of US nuclear weapons in the Baltic country.
- In early July, Lithuania's parliament, the Seimas, began the procedure to repeal Article 137 of the Constitution, which prohibits the stationing of foreign military bases and deployment of nuclear weapons on Lithuanian territory.
- On 9 September, the Seimas Committee on Legal Affairs backed the initiative. Lithuanian Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas stressed that the ban no longer reflects geopolitical realities and that the existing provision makes Lithuania an "outlier" among its Alliance partners when it comes to deterring Russian aggression.
- On 11 September, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov threatened Vilnius, saying that if nuclear weapons are deployed in Lithuania, the country will come under the sights of Russian nuclear weapons.
- Immediately afterwards, Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin claimed that Russia has "never threatened" Europeans and that suggestions of threats from Moscow were fabricated.

articles.title: Iran’s opportunity in BRICS
articles.body:
Iran’s opportunity in BRICS
Jam-e-Jam analyzed the multifaceted importance of BRICS for Iran. It noted that establishing an independent financial system within BRICS is not feasible in the short term, and even among member states there are disagreements about the pace and form of “de‑dollarization.” India has also emphasized that it is not currently seeking a BRICS common currency, focusing instead on cross‑border payments and the use of national currencies.
However, this gradual path can still be valuable for Iran. The more Iran’s trade with regional partners is conducted through local currencies, special accounts, monetary agreements, and independent payment systems, the more a portion of financial sanctions pressure can be neutralized. The key objective is to transform membership into a network of monetary and banking agreements, interconnected payment systems, use of local currencies, financing of joint projects, and ultimately the creation of a regional trade network resistant to sanctions — a network that can reduce the cost and risk of Western financial restrictions on Iran’s economy.
Khorasan: Iran passing through a historic turning point
Khorasan, in an article examining Iran’s current position against adversaries, wrote that West Asia — especially the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz — is now in an extremely complex, historic, and decisive situation. The series of recent events, the developments on the battlefield in Iran’s favor, the strong operational control of Iranian forces over the Strait of Hormuz, the failure of the United States and Israel to achieve any of their declared objectives against Iran, and the decline of America’s standing in global public opinion all point to an undeniable reality: not only has Iran been the victor in this imposed conflict so far, but the distance to achieving final victory — including the removal of US military bases from the region, especially those in Persian Gulf littoral states, and the full implementation of Iranian arrangements over the Strait of Hormuz — is not very great. The article concludes that Iran will successfully navigate this historic and decisive turn, enter a new phase in its national history, demonstrate its power and authority, and firmly consolidate it.
Arman-e-Emrooz: Pakistan’s renewed effort to restart talks
Arman-e-Emrooz discussed Islamabad’s efforts to mediate between Tehran and Washington with the aim of establishing peace. According to the newspaper, Pakistan is seeking to create an environment that can help reduce regional tensions and provide a suitable foundation for constructive dialogue. Pakistan’s defense minister stated that contacts exist between Iranian and American sides, though these communications are indirect and conducted through intermediary channels. These indirect contacts indicate that despite heightened tensions, neither side has completely closed the door on diplomacy, and the possibility of advancing negotiations remains. The main goal is to build mutual trust and reduce misunderstandings so that agreements ensuring regional security can be reached. Lowering tensions would benefit not only Iran and the United States but the entire region — and even the global economy — since instability in this part of the world has cascading effects on energy markets and international trade.
Ettelaat: New technology in naval warfare
Ettelaat reported on Iran’s recent attacks on American targets using missiles equipped with electro‑optical guidance technology. According to the article, instead of relying on satellite systems, these missiles use cameras and optical sensors to identify and track targets. Military experts say that the introduction of such technology into anti‑ship missiles could pose a new threat to US warships, as it reduces the reaction time of defensive systems and complicates target identification. However, the increase in retaliatory attacks — along with attacks on tankers in the region — has raised concerns about safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of the world’s oil shipments transit.
Etemad: Showdown in Vienna
Etemad highlighted the issuance of a resolution against Iran at the IAEA Board of Governors. The newspaper wrote that Western diplomatic pressure in Vienna has intensified. The United States, Britain, France, and Germany have drafted their proposed resolution against Iran and submitted it to the Board; the resolution calls for referring Iran’s case to the UN Security Council and the UN General Assembly. Referring the case does not automatically trigger the return of UN Security Council sanctions, and any new action would face the political balance within the Council — including the positions of China and Russia. Some analysts believe that simultaneous pressure on Iran’s aviation industry, energy exports, and nuclear file has narrowed diplomatic space. Others argue that the expansion of US sanctions on Iran’s aviation sector — alongside rising tensions in Iran’s southern waters and intensified political pressure within the IAEA — shows that Washington is seeking to employ economic, military, and diplomatic tools against Tehran simultaneously. However, Iran’s contacts with regional actors and Qatar’s emphasis on ending the “no war, no peace” situation indicate that the path to dialogue has not been completely closed.

articles.title: Australian Companies to Develop Interceptor Drone for Ukraine
articles.body:
Two companies from South Australia have joined forces to develop and manufacture Arrow interceptor drones for delivery to Ukraine.
This was announced by Chris Picton, Minister for Defence and Space Industry for the State of South Australia.
The agreement calls for the integration of munitions manufactured by Zero Dawn into Praetorian Aeronautics’ Arrow counter-drone system. The system is designed to detect and intercept drones and other unmanned aerial systems in the face of enemy countermeasures.
Under the memorandum, the companies will collaborate on detailed integration, testing, certification, production preparation, and identifying market entry opportunities.
The signing of the memorandum was preceded by tests during which the companies successfully conducted a ground test of the warhead integrated into the interceptor.
The test was observed by Vasyl Myroshnychenko, Ukraine’s ambassador to Australia. Praetorian and Zero Dawn plan to export this system in 2027 to meet Ukraine’s urgent operational needs.
Praetorian Aeronautics is an Australian defense company founded in 2024 that specializes in autonomous aviation systems and software for countering drones.
Praetorian’s current product line consists of the Dagger autonomous interceptor drone, the Venator multi-purpose UAV, and the Hadrian command-and-control system, which uses artificial intelligence to assign targets to interceptors. Currently, there is no publicly available information about the Arrow interceptor or its specifications, so it is likely a new development.
Zero Dawn is an Adelaide-based Australian defense company specializing in the development of modular warheads. It claims to have in-house capabilities in research, design, prototyping, manufacturing, work with explosive materials, and ammunition testing.
The company also develops warheads in collaboration with a specialized partner and claims it can take a project from concept to a tested prototype in 30 days.
As a reminder, since mid-2026, the Australian Defence Force has joined the Norwegian-led multinational Operation Legio to train Ukrainian military personnel in Poland.
Since January 2023, Australian military personnel have been working alongside the multinational training mission Operation Interflex, led by the United Kingdom, as part of Operation Kudu. During this time, they have trained more than 3,650 Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel in basic infantry tactics, leadership, and military skills.

Ukrainian forces struck two chemical industry enterprises in Russia’s Perm and Samara regions and hit multiple military targets in Taganrog over the past 24 hours, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Sept. 12.
“Our long-range responses make the war felt by the aggressor every single day,” Zelensky stated on Facebook.

Zelensky added that earlier Ukrainian strikes this week resulted in the destruction of a Russian Su-33 combat aircraft, two Mi-8 transport helicopters across the Krasnodar and Rostov regions, and an oil facility in Perm.
SBU ‘Alpha’ operation targets drone infrastructure in Taganrog
The strikes in Taganrog, Rostov region, were conducted early Saturday morning by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) in coordination with other branches of the Defense Forces, the intelligence agency reported via Ukrinform.

In the Perm region, roughly 1,500 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, drones targeted the Uralchem-operated Azot plant in Berezniki on Friday, Sept. 11.

articles.title: Zelensky ready to meet Putin at G20 in Miami
articles.body:
Zelensky open to meet Putin at Miami G20 if Russian leader attends
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was willing to meet Russian leader Vladimir Putin at the G20 summit in Miami. However, the Kremlin has not confirmed whether Putin would attend, and it demanded that Zelensky come to Russia for talks instead.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he would be willing to meet Russian leader Vladimir Putin at the G20 summit in Miami for talks on ending the war, in a media interview released Saturday.
But the Kremlin said it had not yet made a decision on whether Putin would attend the gathering of world leaders on December 14-15, and repeated the Russian leader's demand that Zelensky come to Russia for talks.
Putin has repeatedly rejected offers for a face-to-face meeting with Zelensky aimed at brokering an end to more than four years of war.
But the latest offer comes as Washington seeks to kick-start long-stalled talks on Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II, with US negotiators visiting Kyiv and Moscow and President Donald Trump and Putin this week holding talks over the phone.
The United States holds this year's presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, which comprises 19 countries plus the European Union and the African Union, and Russian's finance minister has already attended one G20 meeting.
Read moreZelensky urges Trump to impose new Russia sanctions 'now', after deadly Ukraine strikes
Asked whether he would be willing to meet Putin at the December summit if both leaders were invited, Zelensky told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle: "Yes, of course."
"We have to come. We have to meet, to speak, and make decisions. It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn't matter."
All that mattered were "results", he added.
But Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was cited by Russia's TASS news agency as saying that "we do not know yet whether we will be going to Miami".
Peskov repeated Putin's demand that Zelensky come to Russia – which launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, triggering the war – for any talks: "If he really wants to meet Putin, then Putin has said before that he can fly to Moscow."
In June Zelensky said he had proposed meeting Putin in the United States during a call with Trump, and was waiting to see what came of it.
The Ukrainian leader previously said that Putin ignored an invitation to meet him at a G7 summit in France the same month.
Last weekend, US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv.
Read moreElections in Russia: the 1001 tricks to remove inconvenient candidates
In the Deutsche Welle interview, which took place Friday in Canada, Zelensky said that Witkoff and Kushner's visit was a "good signal", and it was important the pair had made a trip to Kyiv as well as Moscow.
Zelensky has also announced he plans to meet Trump in late September, as Washington pushes for fresh face-to-face talks between Moscow and Kyiv.
'Good position for talks'
Asked about Ukraine's position ahead of possible negotiations, Zelensky responded: "Ukraine now is much more stronger than last year on the battlefield.
"That's why we think that we have now (a) good position for negotiations."
Kyiv has said the talks could happen as early as this month, but the Kremlin on Monday said it was "too early" to discuss a venue or dates.
Several previous rounds of negotiations have failed. Trust between the sides is low, and there is no sign that Moscow or Kyiv have shifted their positions.
Read morePutin arrives in India for BRICS summit set to be dominated by Middle East, Ukraine wars
Both Moscow and Kyiv have escalated long-range strikes on each other in recent months, leading to the highest civilian death toll since the early days of the war.
Overnight Russian strikes killed four people in Ukraine, including two in Zaporizhzhia in the south and two at an ArcelorMittal plant in central Kryvyi Rih, local authorities and the steelmaker said Saturday.
In the interview, Zelensky also repeated his call for Ukraine's allies to provide more missiles to fend off Russian air attacks.
Ukraine urgently needs more interceptor missiles for US-made Patriot air defence systems, but US supplies have been reduced after Washington used large numbers during its war with Iran.
It was not clear whether Washington would provide enough missiles, said Zelensky, adding that they have "political will to sell and to help, but the production is not too big".
He also urged greater help from European allies: "All the Europeans who really support us have what we need."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Second fire in a month hits the Bulgarian plant that ships ammunition to Ukraine, and sabotage is on the table
articles.body:
Fire tore through an ammunition depot belonging to the Bulgarian arms maker EMCO overnight on 12 September, according to RFE/RL. Nobody was hurt, and the interior minister says sabotage is among the versions being examined. It was the second fire at a site of the company, which supplies ammunition to Ukraine, in little over a month.
The warehouses burned one after another
The blaze started near the village of Gorni Varpishta, between Tryavna and Tsareva Livada in Dryanovo municipality. It was visible from Veliko Tarnovo, whose mayor, Daniel Panov, said the fire began around 23:00 on Friday. Gabrovo provincial governor Kristina Sidorova told reporters the fire had taken the depot base and was moving from one store to the next, and she had residents of nearby settlements warned through the BG-Alert emergency system.
Residents nearby heard a series of explosions. Two security guards were the only people on the site and both left in time, Bulgarian media reported. The nearest settlement lies more than a kilometer away, and firefighters ringed the area. EMCO production manager Slavcho Dimiev confirmed to Bulgarian National Television that the store held ammunition and powder, and he told Reuters it mainly contained ammunition, including a small quantity of medium-caliber rounds.
Russia rehearsed how to disable Europe’s undersea communications cables near Svalbard. NATO forces drove them off
Sabotage among the versions
Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said on Saturday the fire was under control and an investigation was running.
"We will review previous cases in which similar fires occurred in the warehouses of this company, as well as at other companies, in order to look for a possible connection or a similar pattern," he said. "We are not ruling out outside interference."
Every ammunition depot in the country will now be inspected, Demerdzhiev said, because storage and security at such sites have been neglected. Dimiev also called for extra protection, saying that if the depots were being targeted, the attack was on the national interest rather than on one company. Lawmaker Bozhidar Bozhanov said the fires are too many and are aimed at one firm, whose owner Russian military intelligence tried to kill, and asked when the state would act.
The owner Russia tried to poison
EMCO belongs to Bulgarian arms trader Emilian Gebrev. He and his plants have been targeted repeatedly in operations attributed to Russian military intelligence over his ammunition deliveries to Ukraine. Gebrev, his son, and a colleague survived a Novichok poisoning attempt in 2015. In 2020 prosecutors charged three Russians whom investigators identified as officers of Russian military intelligence, the GRU.
In 2024 Bulgaria issued arrest warrants for six Russians over EMCO depots destroyed between 2011 and 2020, which held rounds bound for Ukraine and Georgia. Prosecutors said they had grounds to suspect links between those blasts, the poisoning, and the 2014 explosions in Vrbětice, Czechia, that killed two. Moscow denies all of it. Bulgaria supplied Ukraine with weapons until this year's government moved to stop the transfers.
A month earlier, another EMCO site
Explosions and fire hit another EMCO depot on 10 August. Demerdzhiev said at the time that the preliminary version pointed away from external factors.
Founded in 1992, EMCO produces, repairs, and modernizes ammunition and military equipment. The Telegraph reported in late August, citing Western intelligence sources, that Russia had launched a fresh wave of attacks on European defense plants using local criminal groups.
Germany's authorities suspect Russian intelligence behind an arson attack on a defense firm last week, Estonia investigated a suspected arson at a military robot maker supplying Ukraine in August, and Czech police arrested four suspects over a fire at a plant making drones and thermal optics for Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia spent 18 months building the road to Sloviansk. Ukraine spent three taking it back
articles.body:
- Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps has retaken 150–240 sq km north of Lyman since May
- It erased 18 months of Russian groundwork for a northern march on Sloviansk
- Almost nobody reported it for three months—not even Russian war correspondents
- The fighting continues north of Lyman, but on Ukraine's terms
On 22 May, a mechanized battalion of Ukraine's 3rd Assault Brigade—backed by at least two more brigades, the 60th Mechanized and the 66th, attached to the 3rd Army Corps for the operation—attacked Russian positions around the village of Nove, 15 km north of the town of Lyman in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast. Russian drones were heavily jammed that day. Roughly five Ukrainian vehicles were hit, most by fiber-optic drones—the only kind still able to fly.
Nobody outside the Ukrainian army reported it for three months. The first fragmentary accounts surfaced in late August; the full picture only this week. By then the 3rd Army Corps had taken back somewhere between 150 and 240 sq km and wrecked Russian plans for a northern siege of Sloviansk, one of the last two big free cities in Donetsk. Observer Thorkill, writing in Polish, called it a success on an operational scale.
The presence of that Ukrainian armor around Nove, which at the time anchored the right flank of a 100 sq km salient held by regiments of the Russian 20th Combined Arms Army, was an ominous sign for the Russians. After months of careful preparation by the 3rd Army Corps, the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) were strong north of Lyman. Russian forces were weak.
"The moment AFU could start moving vehicles through the area, the battle was basically over," mapper Vitaly wrote three months later. "Vehicles didn't win it, they showed up because the conditions that had made vehicle movement impossible were already gone." Ukrainian drones were everywhere. And Russian drones, effectively jammed by electronic warfare, could barely fly.
Not everyone reads those months the same way. Thorkill, who tracked the sector throughout, puts the breakthrough at 17 to 18 August, and writes that for most of July and early August the 3rd Corps' attacks were repelled by the Russian 144th Motor Rifle Division. On that account the slow months were not a steady advance. What turned them, he says, is not clear: someone on the Ukrainian side made the difference north of Kolodiazi. He is candid about the limits of what can be seen. Some sources say the Russians withdrew, others deny it, others say they were partly cut off. What he can confirm from satellite imagery is that Ukrainian forces retook Serednie and Zelena Dolyna.
Overextended and pummeled by drones, the Russians barely clung to their salient north of Lyman, which sat between the Nitrius and Zherebets rivers. They were especially exposed at its western edge, where they had pushed across the Nitrius. The Russians had hoped the salient would be a "base for an offensive on Lyman, which could have allowed further offensives to Izium and Sloviansk [and] threatened the northern supply road to Donbas," according to mapper Clément Molin.
Instead, the salient became a trap as the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps relentlessly—but quietly—exploited the fragility of the Russian 20th Combined Arms Army. The Russians have now been pushed back toward the Zherebets, leaving behind their uncounted dead ... and their ambitions for a quick northern march on Lyman and then Sloviansk and neighboring Kramatorsk.
It had taken Russian forces 18 months to set the conditions for a push toward Sloviansk from the north. In the three months beginning with that mechanized assault around Nove, the Russians "apparently lost 1.5 years of progress in the area," Vitaly concluded. Estimates of the ground retaken vary: Molin puts it at more than 200 sq km, the AKM Mapping account at 151, and Konrad Muzyka of Rochan Consulting at around 240.
The appearance of Ukrainian armor around Nove in late May was a strong indication that the 3rd Army Corps had the momentum. But that doesn't mean the Corps' eventual victory in the battle for the Lyman salient was a foregone conclusion. On paper, the Russians have a manpower and firepower advantage in Donetsk.
A bridgehead too far
The 20th Combined Arms Army advanced too far, too fast. And the terrain favored the Ukrainian defenders, who could pluck at the Russians' supply lines from entrenched positions until the time was right for a counterattack.
"Russia putting itself inside a deep, narrow pocket only made the final phase easier," Vitaly explained. "Once AFU had enough control over the surrounding movement, every new Russian mission sent into the area walked into a reinforced perception trap—troops committed to hold positions that existed far more convincingly in reports than as a functioning front."
The silence
What kept the trap working was that nobody talked about it. The Ukrainian general staff said nothing. Pro-Ukrainian analysts, who normally map every advance within hours, held their tongues until late August. So did the Russians.
Observer Andrew Perpetua, who has followed Ukraine's other quiet operations around Kupiansk and in southern Donetsk, called this one tighter still. The Lyman operation "seemed even more protected since even the most in the know and honest Russian reporters seem to be missing it. Or at least silent about it," he wrote. "It was honestly shocking to watch how out of the loop the Russians really were, which I think is in large part due to the collective action of OSINT to avoid speaking about the situation."
Perpetua's reading is that the lying is heaviest exactly where Russian forces are being pushed back. Nearby Sviatohirsk is the case in point. Vladimir Putin recently announced its capture. On 7 September, the commander of the 3rd Army Corps, Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, walked around the town on camera.
The 3rd Army Corps cut across the salient around three weeks ago, reaching the northern edge of Kolodiazi and trapping an unknown number of Russian stragglers between the Ukrainian vanguard and the old Russian bridgehead. Most of the encircled Russians appear to have escaped. "There is a large area where there may still be Russian soldiers," Molin warned. "Most of the villages westwards have been cleared, but not the treelines."
On 24 August the Ukrainians mounted a second mechanized attack, so the operation has not stopped. But the 3rd Army Corps is likely shifting from attacking to consolidating and defending—and clearing out the Russian stragglers that, left alone, could sow chaos in the new gray zone that was once a Russian salient.
Russian channels have started to admit the problem. Rybar wrote of "problems near Lyman," conceding that Ukrainian units have been attacking southward from Ridkodub for months and that Russian forces "do not even control the airspace immediately near the front line." The fighting continues, but on Ukraine's terms, for now.
How much it changes is the one thing the analysts do not agree on. "This is one of the most important victory for Ukraine in 2026," Molin wrote, a victory that "will delay the offensive on northern Donbas." Thorkill, in the same post that called it an operational-scale success and rated it larger than the 7th Rapid Reaction Corps' gains near Velyka Novosilka in July, ends on the opposite note: it will not, he writes, affect in any way the situation of Ukrainian forces on the direction that matters most at present, the Kramatorsk agglomeration.

articles.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy offers to meet Putin at G20 summit in December
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin at a G20 summit in December, in an interview released on Saturday, as efforts intensify to end the conflict.
Washington is seeking to kick-start long-stalled negotiations to find a solution to the conflict, Europe's deadliest since World War II, with US negotiators recently visiting Kiev and Moscow and President Donald Trump and Putin this week holding talks on the conflict over the phone.
The United States holds this year's presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, which comprises 19 countries plus the European Union and the African Union, and culminates in a leaders' summit in Miami in December.
Russia's finance minister has already attended one G20 meeting, causing discomfort among some of Ukraine's allies, and a Russian diplomat said on Saturday that Moscow will also send some officials to a G20 energy meeting in Houston next week.
Asked whether he would be willing to meet Putin at the December summit if both leaders were invited, Zelenskyy told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle: "Yes, of course.
"We have to come. We have to meet, to speak, and make decisions.
"It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn't matter. It doesn't matter. Matters only result. Result matters. That's it."
Last weekend, US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Putin and Trump also discussed the war earlier in the week in what the Kremlin termed an "extremely frank" and constructive hour-long phone call.
Diplomatic efforts intensify
In the Deutsche Welle interview, which took place Friday in Canada, Zelenskyy said that Witkoff and Kushner's visit was a "good signal", and it was important the pair had visited Kiev as well as Moscow.
"It's respect to our people," he said.
Zelenskyy has also announced he plans to meet Trump in late September, as Washington pushes for fresh face-to-face talks between Moscow and Kiev.
Asked about Ukraine's position ahead of possible negotiations, Zelenskyy responded: "Ukraine now is much more stronger than last year on the battlefield."
Russia was sustaining heavy battlefield losses, paying a "big price" for "very slow moves on the battlefield," he said.
"That's why we think that we have now good position for negotiations."
Kiev has said the talks could happen as early as this month, but the Kremlin on Monday said it was "too early" to discuss a venue or dates.
Several previous rounds of negotiations have failed. Trust between the sides is low, and there is no sign that Moscow or Kiev have shifted their positions.
Both Moscow and Kiev have escalated long-range strikes on each other in recent months, leading to the highest civilian death toll since the early days of the war.
Zelenskyy also repeated his call for Ukraine's allies to provide more interceptor missiles to fend off Russian air attacks.
"Russia produces... today 140 ballistic missiles per month. So, according to the rules of NATO, if you want to destroy 140, you need 280... You will never have 280 missiles per month," he said.
It was a "huge challenge" to have 100 a month, he said.

articles.title: Drone crashes near Suceava in Romania
articles.body:
Drone crashes near Suceava in Romania
A crashed drone was found in a cornfield in the Botoșenița Mare area of Suceava County, Romania, on the afternoon of 12 September.
Source: Romanian Ministry of National Defence, as reported by European Pravda citing Digi24
Details: The drone's impact with the ground caused a small fire and left a crater approximately one metre in diameter.
Earlier, the authorities sent an RO-Alert message to Suceava County after Ukraine and Moldova reported the presence of a drone.
"On Saturday, 12 September, the Air Operations Control Centres of Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova informed the Ministry of National Defence that a drone had crossed the airspace of both countries, heading towards north-eastern Romania. Two Romanian Air Force F-16 aircraft took off from the 86th Air Base in Borcea to monitor the situation," the Romanian Ministry of National Defence said.
The National Military Command Centre informed the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations that public warning measures were being introduced in Botoșani County, sending an RO-Alert message at 16:20. At the same time, the 112 emergency service received a report of a drone over the village of Știubieni in Botoșani County.
"Following reconnaissance conducted by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, an aircraft that had crashed was found in a cornfield in the Botoșenița Mare area of Suceava County. The impact caused a small fire and left a crater approximately one metre in diameter and 30 cm deep. No casualties were reported. A pyrotechnics team from the Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) is heading to the scene to assess the situation," the Ministry of Defence said.
Background:
- In Romania, debris from numerous UAVs was found throughout 11 September, with some of the drones carrying warheads.
- On 10 September, drone wreckage was also found on a beach in Romania.
- On the morning of 11 September, Romania scrambled F-16 fighter jets to monitor aerial assets near the border with Ukraine.

Drones Strike Russian Aviation Plant Servicing Tu-95 Bombers and Chemical Giant in Tolyatti
Drone attacks struck industrial and military facilities in the Russian cities of Taganrog and Tolyatti overnight on September 12, with fires reported near an aircraft complex that services A-50 surveillance planes and Tu-95 strategic bombers, as well as at one of Russia’s major chemical producers.
