According to Exilenova+ on September 12, satellite fire-detection data and footage shared by local residents showed several fires in Taganrog, including near the Beriev Taganrog Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex.
The facility specializes in maintenance and modernization of Russia’s A-50 airborne early warning and control aircraft, Be-series amphibious aircraft used by the Russian Navy, and Tu-95MS/MSM strategic bombers. Russia uses Tu-95 bombers to launch Kh-101 air-launched cruise missiles against Ukraine.

articles.title: Zelensky Warns of Reciprocal Strikes if Russia Targets Power Grid
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Ukraine will retaliate in kind if Russian forces launch strikes against the country’s energy infrastructure this winter, pledging reciprocal consequences if Moscow attempts to plunge Ukrainian cities into blackouts.
Speaking in an interview with American journalist Fareed Zakaria and addressing the Yalta European Strategy (YES) forum in Kyiv on Friday, Sept. 11, Zelensky stressed that while Russia is preparing an aerial campaign against Ukraine’s power grid, Kyiv has built the capabilities to respond symmetrically.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Ukraine is capable of responding to Russia for any of their operations,” Zelensky said. “Russia knows that if they strike – and they are preparing to strike our energy system in the winter – Russia will receive the exact same. If they cause us blackouts, we will try to respond to them in kind.”
Zelensky clarified that while Kyiv will not emulate Moscow’s disregard for civilian life, it will not leave strategic infrastructure attacks unanswered. “I’m not comparing this to the humanitarian catastrophes they are causing today. Ukraine does not do that,” he stated.
Call for an ‘energy truce’
Zelensky emphasized that an escalating cycle of infrastructure strikes can be averted if the parties agree to a targeted “energy truce” alongside unblocking the Black Sea.
“The negotiation process must be about ending the war,” Zelensky explained. “And if Russia does not want to end it, then partners need to find an approach toward it. If that is difficult to find, then today, at the very least, we need to move forward step by step. Unblock the Black Sea and find a way toward an energy truce, if one can use that phrase, where the energy sector of both countries is protected.”
Russian Missile-Drone Attack Hits Odesa Apartment Building, Injures Six
“In other words, if the Russians do not strike our energy system – and our people have electricity – Ukraine will likewise refrain from responding,” the president added.
Addressing the broader geopolitical spillovers of the conflict, Zelensky raised alarm over the maritime food corridor in the Black Sea, which remains heavily obstructed from both sides due to ongoing strikes on civilian commercial vessels and port facilities.
While assuring that domestic food security is not under threat, Zelensky warned that the naval deadlock poses catastrophic risks for the Global South, comparing the situation to maritime bottlenecks in the Middle East.
“Ukrainians will not be left without food,” Zelensky said.
“Grain prices will fall [domestically] because exporting will be expensive, commercial infrastructure will be complicated, and logistics will be terrible. But beyond Ukraine, other nations will be in a far worse situation where they simply will not have food. Many peoples will have nothing to eat, even if they have money. That will be Hormuz, but agricultural. And this is a grave problem that cannot be solved by Ukraine alone.”
Zelensky noted that he has conducted direct consultations regarding maritime food transport with leaders from Egypt, India, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.
Step-by-step diplomacy and push for US sanctions
Framing energy protection and food transit as the two most urgent global challenges stemming from the war, Zelensky reiterated that diplomacy remains Ukraine’s preferred avenue, urging international partners to help organize a formal trilateral negotiation format alongside ongoing prisoner exchanges.
Concurrently, the president appealed to the US to accelerate the adoption of a sweeping new sanctions package against the Russian Federation, specifically commending legislative efforts linked to US Senator Lindsey Graham.
“Sanctions need to be introduced now. Sanctions must be strong,” Zelensky urged. “During a war, it is better to make an imperfect decision at times than to do nothing at all.”

articles.title: Germany Wants to Prevent the Far-Right AfD from Accessing Secret War Plan
articles.body:
Germany plans to deny an entire region’s government access to a secret defense plan if the far-right AfD comes to power in the elections.
This was reported by Bloomberg.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius wants to ensure that the state government of Saxony-Anhalt, led by the pro-Russian “Alternative for Germany” (AfD), cannot pass on details of the plan to Russia.
OPLAN is 1,000 pages long and outlines a defense plan developed by German authorities and NATO in the event of war or a crisis. It calls for coordinated action by federal and regional authorities.
According to the publication’s source, Pistorius outlined his intentions on Tuesday during a closed-door meeting with defense policy experts from the parliamentary factions of the governing coalition. The source spoke on condition of anonymity because the discussions were not public. Decision-makers speculate that OPLAN could be activated in the event of an escalation with Russia.
The plan is based on Germany’s central geographical location as a logistics hub for NATO troops, who would be deployed eastward if the defense of the North Atlantic Alliance were necessary. The full version of the OPLAN is available to the leaders of all 16 German states, while local authorities have access only to select parts of the overall plan.
German officials have been discussing for several months how to protect sensitive information in the event that a far-right party gains control over security agencies at the state level. Among the possible options is the deletion or classification of certain data, Bloomberg News reported in July.
The AfD, which Germany’s domestic intelligence agency partially considers a threat to the country’s constitutional order, won 44% of the vote, securing 39 of 83 seats in the Saxony-Anhalt election. The party fell just three seats short of an absolute majority in the state parliament.
If negotiations to form a coalition with the pro-Russian far-left party BSW, which won five seats and was the only party willing to discuss cooperation, are successful, such a coalition could bring the far right to power in one of Germany’s regions for the first time since World War II.
In late March, European diplomats and German lawmakers had already warned that the “Alternative for Germany” (AfD) party could be passing confidential information from internal EU databases to Russia.
This involves access to thousands of documents, including the minutes of closed-door meetings of ambassadors where plans to finance Ukraine using frozen Russian assets were discussed. Representatives of Germany’s ruling parties note that AfD politicians are attempting to obtain, through parliamentary inquiries, information on drone defense, transport routes for Western weapons to Ukraine, and measures to counter Russian sabotage. The party itself officially denies the espionage allegations and calls them baseless.
In early July, AfD member Noah Krieger (also known as Murat Dadaev) joined the Russian army and announced the formation of a battalion in Russia that will consist of Germans.

Russian attacks kill 11, injure 96 across Ukraine as Odesa comes under mass overnight strike
At least 11 people were killed and 96 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, as Moscow launched a mass overnight missile and drone attack targeting Odesa Oblast, local authorities said on Sept. 12.
In Odesa Oblast, at least 35 people were injured, including a five-month-old infant and a 17-year-old, local Governor Oleh Kiper said.
"The enemy attacked the city. A multi-story residential building was damaged," Kiper said as the first consequences of the strike emerged.
Russia launched 129 attack drones of various types overnight, including Shahed-type and jet-powered drones, as well as eight Kalibr cruise missiles, six Kh-59/69 guided missiles, and Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, the Air Force said. Ukrainian forces shot down 110 targets, with hits recorded at 20 locations and debris from intercepted targets falling at four additional sites.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, two people were killed and at least 22 others injured, including a child, local Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. In Dnipro, one person was killed and 19 injured as Russian drones, artillery, and aerial bombs damaged an enterprise, apartment buildings, garages, and vehicles.
Overnight, another person was killed and three injured in Kryvyi Rih after Russian forces struck an industrial enterprise. A 54-year-old man was hospitalized in serious condition, Hanzha added.
In Donetsk Oblast, four people were killed and five injured in Russian attacks over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Two people were killed in Sloviansk, while one person was killed in Kramatorsk and another in Yasnohirka.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two people were killed and 11 injured in Russian attacks, Governor Ivan Fedorov said. Russian forces carried out 1,001 strikes against 45 settlements in the region over the past day, including five missile strikes on the city of Zaporizhzhia, according to Fedorov.
In Kyiv Oblast, one person was killed and three others injured, including a child, as Russian strike drones hit five districts over the past day, local authorities said. Damage was recorded in the Brovary, Obukhiv, Bucha, Boryspil, and Vyshhorod districts. Fifteen sites were damaged, including seven homes, vehicles, warehouses, hangars, and a power line.
In Sumy Oblast, a 68-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone strike on the Myropillia community, while a 64-year-old man was injured in a separate drone attack on the Novoslobidska community, local authorities said. Russian forces carried out more than 50 attacks against 25 settlements in Sumy Oblast over the past day, using artillery, mortars, FPV drones, other unmanned aircraft, and guided aerial bombs.
In Kharkiv Oblast, a 32-year-old man was killed in an attack on Kharkiv, while a 19-year-old man was injured elsewhere in the region, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russian forces attacked Kharkiv and seven other settlements using guided aerial bombs and multiple types of drones.
In Kherson Oblast, 18 people were injured in Russian attacks targeting residential areas as well as critical and social infrastructure, local authorities said. Fifteen apartment buildings were damaged, along with shops, a gas station, a service station, an ambulance, and vehicles.
Russian Shahed-type drones also struck railway infrastructure in Lutsk, Volyn Oblast, and Fastiv in Kyiv Oblast, Ukrzaliznytsia said. No passengers were injured after monitoring teams detected the threat in time and evacuated them, according to the state railway operator.

articles.title: Russian Hackers Used Claude AI to Launch Attacks Against Ukraine and Europe
articles.body:
The Russian hacking group Midnight Blizzard used Claude, an AI developed by Anthropic, to automate cyberespionage operations against Ukraine and European countries.
Anthropic reported this in its report titled “Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI: September 2026.”
According to the researchers, from December 2025 to August 2026, the hackers attacked more than 20 organizations. Targets included government, military, and intelligence agencies; diplomatic missions; think tanks; defense companies; and drone manufacturers.
Claude was used in nearly every stage of the attacks: to identify potential targets, gather information, register domains, set up phishing infrastructure, steal credentials, move laterally within compromised networks, and exfiltrate hundreds of gigabytes of data.
Російські хакери використали ШІ Claude для атак на Україну та Європу pic.twitter.com/4CBP6Ugcxr
— dimdim (@dimdim518484) September 11, 2026
The AI also monitored whether security systems were detecting the group’s malicious programs. If an antivirus detected one of them, the system analyzed the reason for the detection, modified the code, and recompiled the program until it became invisible to security measures.
The attackers paid particular attention to drone technologies and related supply chains. They dumped the contents of email inboxes belonging to at least two drone component manufacturers, attacked a manufacturer of military UAVs, and stole a set of development tools for proprietary software used in a drone’s machine vision system.
Over the course of several days, the attackers reverse-engineered the stolen software. They reconstructed the system’s architecture, the list of hardware components, information about suppliers, and details about a product that had not yet been released.
To gain indirect access to priority targets, the group compromised at least three hotel Wi-Fi providers. By modifying DNS records, the hackers redirected guests’ devices to servers under their control and distributed malware for Windows, Android, and iOS.
The attackers also gained access to WhatsApp accounts. To do this, they used a browser-based platform without a graphical user interface, which connected devices controlled by the attackers to the victims’ accounts as linked devices.
The setup, partially built on the open-source WhatsApp automation library WPPConnect, disabled read receipts. As a result, victims did not notice the mass download of their correspondence in Ukrainian and Russian. At least two former high-ranking Ukrainian officials were targeted in this manner.
The group also targeted video surveillance platforms. The attackers identified authorization vulnerabilities in the application programming interfaces (APIs) of video streaming services from cameras. By exploiting these vulnerabilities, they obtained user lists and stole tokens that granted access to live streams from the victims’ cameras.
The same group infiltrated the systems of a government technology agency in a North African country. The attackers stole the entire database of account records, which contained over 300,000 entries from the national citizen identification system, as well as data from the commercial registry on more than half a million companies operating in the country.
As a reminder, in July it was revealed that a group of Russian hackers had been conducting a cyberespionage campaign over the past year targeting American scientists in the nuclear sector, defense contractors, and government officials.

Modi and Putin have agreed to strengthen India-Russia ties, says Reuters
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin have agreed to deepen bilateral ties during talks in New Delhi ahead of a BRICS summit.
Source: Reuters
Details: The talks took place ahead of a BRICS summit due to be attended by Chinese leader Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa.
India's Ministry of External Affairs said Modi and Putin had exchanged assessments of conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region that affect commercial shipping and the safety of Indian sailors.
"The two leaders agreed to remain engaged in an effort to strengthen further the special and privileged strategic partnership between the two countries," it noted.
The two countries also announced plans to increase bilateral trade from nearly US$70 billion in 2024-2025 to US$100 billion by 2030.
Speaking at a BRICS business forum event, Putin complained about pressure from Western countries.
"We have always been told that competition is a sacred cow, something that must not be touched. Yet, unfortunately, today your Western competitors are trying by any means necessary to regain their former leadership," he said.
He added that the confrontation has escalated to "direct physical attacks or the destruction of industrial and logistical facilities, pipelines, and so forth", the blocking of vessels and threats to impose secondary sanctions.
Kirill Dmitriev, one of Putin's envoys, said BRICS is evolving from a geopolitical grouping into a more practical economic partnership focused on developing infrastructure, business and payment systems.
Meanwhile, finance ministers and central bank heads from BRICS member states expressed concern over unilateral trade restrictions and tariffs that contravene World Trade Organization (WTO) rules.
India, along with China, remains one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil, providing Moscow with revenue to finance its war against Ukraine.
Background:
- In July 2024, Modi visited Moscow to meet Putin. On the same day, Russia launched a large-scale missile strike on the Okhmatdyt National Children's Specialised Hospital in Kyiv.

articles.title: ‘Explosive’ planes and bioweapons: CIA declassifies pre-9/11 intel warnings
articles.body:
‘Explosive’ planes and bioweapons: CIA declassifies pre-9/11 intel warnings
The CIA has declassified dozens of presidential intelligence briefings revealing that US officials were warned years before the September 11 attacks that Osama bin Laden and his Al-Qaeda network were considering strikes on American soil involving hijacked or explosive-packed aircraft, while also pursuing biological, chemical, and nuclear weapons.
The agency released 71 President’s Daily Brief (PDB) products on Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11. The collection, totaling more than 100 pages, is the largest release of CIA presidential intelligence related to the attacks and covers assessments dating from 1998 through the immediate aftermath of September 11, 2001.
Among the most striking documents is a September 1998 memorandum on Bin Laden’s intentions. Intelligence indicated that his “preferred option” was to strike the US “on its own soil in Washington,” the CIA wrote, warning that his network “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city.”

Three months later, another briefing warned that Bin Laden and his allies were preparing attacks in the US, including a plan to hijack an American airliner during the holiday season.

A February 1998 assessment claimed Bin Laden and other extremists sought to procure unspecified chemical, biological, and nuclear substances. By May 1999, the CIA assessed that Bin Laden was pursuing “a variety of options” for developing these types of weapons. A subsequent briefing in June said trainees at an Afghan camp produced and tested “dozens of toxic chemicals and biological toxins,” and that operatives experimented with adding radioactive material to explosives.
The best-known warning came on August 6, 2001, when then-President George W. Bush received a briefing titled ‘Bin Ladin Determined To Strike in US’. It said Bin Laden had wanted to attack the US for years, cited suspicious activity consistent with preparations for hijackings, and noted that the FBI was conducting around 70 investigations into possible Al-Qaeda-linked activity in the country.
By the summer of 2001, then-CIA Director George Tenet later recalled, the intelligence system was “blinking red.”
The 9/11 Commission found that many officials knew “something terrible was planned,” but failures in intelligence sharing, policy, and preparedness prevented the scattered warnings from being turned into action.
Bin Laden rose to prominence during the Soviet war in Afghanistan, when Washington poured billions of dollars into arming anti-Soviet mujahideen through Pakistan. US officials have denied directly funding Bin Laden, but the American-backed war helped create the militant infrastructure and environment from which Al-Qaeda later emerged.
The deadliest terrorist attack in US history, which killed 2,977 people, prompted Washington to launch the War on Terror, invading Afghanistan within weeks and Iraq less than two years later. At home, the PATRIOT Act vastly expanded the government’s powers to spy on its own citizens.

articles.title: Fast kill but also long game: Russia is using AI-generated women and long conversations to lure Ukrainian soldiers to their deaths
articles.body:
Russia is using AI-generated women to lure Ukrainian soldiers to their deaths. The fabricated profiles are one of three versions of a "honey trap" scheme Russia has escalated this year, and Ukraine's military counterintelligence has foiled more than 50 such attempts in 2026, said Artem Dekhtiarenko, spokesperson for the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU).
In an army of more than a million, six soldiers have been killed this way, cases Dekhtiarenko called isolated but real, and Russia will spend months grooming a fake romance for a single one of them. It has revived a classic Soviet tactic, but not to compromise soldiers as the KGB once did. The aim now is to kill them and to spread the panic that makes the war feel uncontrolled.
The scheme runs in three versions
The first relies on technology. Artificial intelligence can now generate a woman's photos convincingly enough that, without close analysis, it is hard to tell whether she exists, Dekhtiarenko said.
The second uses real women living in occupied territory who work for Russia's services.
The third, and rarest, uses women on Ukrainian-held ground who agree to help and are eventually caught.
"There is an inevitability of punishment," Dekhtiarenko said, adding that the SBU and police will detain every agent, and the sentences are severe.
Russia plays the long game
The traps are not always quick. Russia wants to recruit, use a target, and move on quickly, Dekhtiarenko explained, but investigators have logged correspondence that spanned months of steady messaging before the strike. That patience is itself a warning to soldiers, he added, and reason to watch such contacts carefully.
The killings aim to sow panic
Asked why Russia would spend so much on a single soldier, Dekhtiarenko said the goal is psychological: to sow panic, destabilize, and make the situation look beyond Ukraine's control.

articles.title: US believes Iran used Chinese satellite images for Jordan attack
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US believes Iran used Chinese satellite images for Jordan airbase strike
US officials believe that Iran obtained high resolution satellite images from Chinese sources before carrying out an attack on Jordan's Muwaffaq Salti airbase in July, killing three American soldiers, The Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday.
The unnamed officials described the intelligence as the "clearest" evidence of Chinese support for Tehran during the US-Israeli war launched in late February.
The officials declined to identify which Chinese entity had provided the satellite images, and stopped short of accusing Beijing of direct involvement. Sources indicated that senior US officials raised the issue with their Chinese counterparts, who dismissed the concerns and denied the involvement of Chinese firms.
The US believes that Iran acquired images of both before and after the attack, according to the report.
The report also quoted informed sources as saying that Washington is concerned about the possibility of Beijing assisting Iran in tracking US naval vessels. Iran has in recent days launched ballistic missiles toward a US aircraft carrier and other warships in the region. US Central Command (CENTCOM) said that the attacks missed their target, however sources who spoke to the WSJ said the strikes came "close".
Officials told the US news outlet that the Trump administration had in recent weeks briefed congressional intelligence committees on information relating to Russian and Chinese support for Iran.
In July, Trump warned Russia and China against interfering in the war with Iran, though said he did not believe that the two countries were "involved". The president added that his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping had assured him during his visit to Beijing that China would not supply or sell weapons to Iran.

articles.title: Washington eyes foreign warships from Japan, South Korea, Turkey amid China naval threat
articles.body:
About a century ago, Congress barred the US Navy from buying ships from foreign shipyards to protect the American shipbuilding industry and preserve domestic capabilities. But growing concerns over China’s rapidly expanding navy and the aging of the US fleet are now pushing Washington to reconsider that long-standing policy.
The United States has struggled to reach its goal of maintaining 300 operational warships, while China’s navy has expanded to around 400 vessels. Beijing’s fleet also increasingly includes modern ships that represent a significant advance over earlier generations.
The US Defense Department is expected to issue its first tender in October for the purchase of frigates from foreign shipyards. Under the plan, foreign shipbuilders could construct some of the vessels themselves while helping train American shipyards to build additional ships in the future, a move intended to reduce costs and speed up production.
The tender is expected to include ships from two close US allies, South Korea and Japan. Japan, which fought against the United States during World War II, became a US ally after the war ended 81 years ago with the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
A third contender is also expected to join the competition. After a conversation between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and US President Donald Trump at last month’s NATO summit, Turkey will also participate in the tender.
Over the past decade, Erdogan has invested billions of dollars in Turkey’s domestic defense industry, which has expanded into advanced shipbuilding capabilities. However, security ties between Washington and Ankara remain complicated.
Turkey has not been returned to the F-35 fighter jet program despite Erdogan’s efforts after being removed from the project over its purchase of Russian air defense systems. The US argued that the systems could have exposed sensitive information about the aircraft’s stealth capabilities.
Erdogan also prevented the US from launching attacks against Iran from Turkish territory. Despite those tensions, Trump agreed to provide Turkey with jet engines for the Kaan stealth fighter aircraft that Ankara is developing.
The US has never previously purchased Turkish weapons systems, unlike its defense acquisitions from Israel. A decision to purchase Turkish-built naval vessels would therefore represent a significant step forward in the defense relationship between the two countries.
It remains unclear whether Trump could secure congressional approval for a multibillion-dollar purchase from Turkey.
Turkey’s Istanbul-class frigate
The Istanbul-class frigate that Turkey is expected to offer is smaller than its competitors, measuring 113 meters in length with a displacement of approximately 3,100 tons.
The vessel is equipped with 16 modular vertical launch system (VLS) cells, a 76 mm main gun, locally produced Atmaca anti-ship missiles, and a Phalanx close-in weapon system.
Its radar is based on an AESA system developed by Turkish defense company Aselsan.
The frigate’s main advantages are its lower production costs and the availability of multiple production lines at private shipyards across Turkey. Turkey has already ordered eight vessels of the class, while Indonesia has ordered two.
South Korea’s Chungnam-class frigate
South Korea’s Chungnam-class frigate is larger and heavier than the Turkish vessel, measuring approximately 130 meters in length with a displacement of around 4,300 tons.
The frigate is armed with a 127 mm (5-inch) gun, 16 vertical launch cells, and a multifunction AESA radar integrated into an advanced electronic mast.
South Korea’s main advantage lies in the industrial capabilities of major shipbuilders HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean, which can produce warships at a rapid pace.
South Korea has ordered six vessels of the class so far.
Japan’s Mogami-class frigate
Japan’s Mogami-class frigate is the largest and most heavily armed of the three competitors. The vessel ranges from 133 to 142 meters in length and has a displacement of approximately 5,500 tons.
Its weapons systems include a 127 mm (5-inch) gun, 16 to 32 Mk 41 vertical launch cells, and Type 17 missiles.
The frigate is notable for its advanced enclosed stealth mast, known as UNICORN, which is integrated with an AESA radar system.
Its main advantage is its high level of automation, allowing the ship to operate with only about 90 crew members, roughly half the number typically required for comparable Western frigates.
Japan has ordered 10 ships of the class.

articles.title: Ukraine’s parliament changes how military budget is cleared, and freezes money behind one of war’s cleverest supply schemes, defense-industry council says
articles.body:
New changes to the legislation from Ukraine's parliament have jammed the money in one of the war's cleverest supply schemes: the system that lets frontline units turn confirmed kills into new weapons. Under the program, known as eBaly, a military unit can earn points for verified strikes on Russian targets and spend them on Ukrainian-made drones and other gear, which the makers deliver first and get paid for later. The makers have kept delivering. The payments have stopped, according to Ihor Fedirko, who runs the Ukrainian Council of Defense Industry.
The freeze is real money to real firms. Fedirko says the companies are owed between $540,000 and several million dollars each for equipment already handed over and have gone roughly two months without payment. It matters because eBaly is not a fringe experiment: units have ordered and received more than 181,000 drones, robots, and electronic-warfare systems through it in 2026, choosing the gear that performs best in combat.
The Ukrainian Council of Defense Industry brings together more than 300 private manufacturers and key associations of Ukraine’s defense-industrial sector.
A budget change froze the money
The problem, Fedirko said, affects every delivery made through eBaly. Under the updated 2026 budget, the split of Ukraine's military income tax stayed the same: 60 percent to the Defense Ministry, 30 percent to the state communications service, and 10 percent straight to military units.
But the ministry's and the communications service's shares now have to be signed off by the Ukrainian National Security Committee.
"Now, the committee approves not individual payments or deliveries but the general directions of spending," Fedirko wrote.
It is unclear what is causing such delays in obtaining signatures on committee decisions and what is lacking to enable swift decision-making.
It is worth noting that the Ebaly system reduces the risk of ministries approving procurement through “their own” companies, since hundreds of companies participate in it and are selected by hundreds of commanders.
Small firms feel it first
For the largest defense companies, a delay of a million or two dollars is a manageable cash-flow gap, Fedirko said. For small ones, the same money was meant to cover wages, buy components, and fund the next production run.
"Some enterprises have already run into problems paying salaries," he wrote.
Producers have spent about two months appealing to the responsible institutions to clear the debt for gear already delivered, without result.

articles.title: Are the UK sanctions on Israel real progress, or more illusion?
articles.body:
The United Kingdom, joined by Canada and France, announced this week that they are taking action against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. It’s an announcement that is at once groundbreaking and insufficient.
Specifically, the UK said it would suspend export licenses for weapons materially supporting Israel’s illegal occupation; ban imports of Israeli settlement goods, and; sanction private companies providing services–including financial services–that enable settlement expansion.
Those are, without a doubt, positive steps. They break with the long-standing western practice of empty condemnations of settlement activity without establishing any consequences if Israel continues that activity.
The fact that the sanctions the UK announced could include firms that provide services that support the expansion of settlements is also a meaningful and groundbreaking step. It widens the scope of actions that can be taken to prevent settlement expansion to areas that are much easier to influence than Israeli settlers themselves, especially in the field of finance.
In explaining these sanctions to the House of Commons, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband bolstered accusations of war crimes against Israel and even described its actions on the West Bank as “ethnic cleansing.”
That is perhaps the most important development here. A major ally of Israel, one which is often said to have its own “special relationship” with the United States, is supporting the decision of the International Court of Justice that declared Israel’s occupation of the West Bank and Gaza illegal.
That could profoundly change the international discourse regarding the politics around not just settlements but the occupation as a whole.
These are unquestionably good things, and represent real progress, coming from a sector that has been so complicit with Israeli crimes and so hypocritical in ignoring the yawning gap between British rhetoric on the issue and its actions.
But the enthusiasm in some quarters over this announcement is overblown. There is a need to pump the brakes and prepare for a much greater push that can capitalize on this promising first step, address its shortcomings, and create something impactful.
What’s missing in the UK statement
Obviously, we cannot expect the United Kingdom to go from a regressive, genocide-enabling policy to one that promotes real justice and hope in one day. Since that is too much to ask, we need to be clear-eyed about what is still needed, not to chastise Miliband or his new boss, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, but to encourage and push them to go much further.
The exclusive targeting of settlements means that expansion will be more costly for Israel and that settlement enterprises themselves would face barriers to their income.
That’s great, but it is also already international law and, ostensibly, the policy of both the UK and the European Union. The problem is not the rules, it’s their enforcement.
The sanctions on settlements will not go into effect for six to nine months, and we can be sure that legal and political challenges will be mounted by Israel and its British supporters to maximize the delay.
During that time, the momentum and political urgency driven by this announcement could fade. If it becomes less politically convenient to enforce the sanctions, it would be very much in keeping with long-standing British and European practice to ignore them.
Then there is the matter of the efficacy of sanctioning only the settlements, not the state.
Back in June, the Global Echo Litigation Center released an illuminating report detailing the many ways settlement products evade regulations on labeling their point of origin accurately, making it more difficult to police their sale. It’s a system that is easily gamed.
As I reported at the time, “For years, it’s been widely known that Israel exports products, chiefly agricultural, from its settlements on the West Bank and the Golan Heights under a ‘Made in Israel’ label. It does so even though it is legally required by the European Union and the United Kingdom to label such products as being from settlements.”
Given the volume of world events and the speed of the news cycle these days, it is easy to imagine that, in nine months or more, the burden of policing false labeling and other deceptive practices would be more than the UK would want to undertake.
It’s also important to note that the ban on weapons is somewhat selective. One of the most crucial items Israel imports from the UK, albeit indirectly, are components of the F-35 fighter jet, a plane commonly used for airstrikes in Gaza. Those components were excluded from the weapons ban.
Indeed, Miliband’s wording on weaponry in general was very vague. “We will now also refuse all license applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation…”
Like cutting off money to the settlements, arms sales are fungible. Many arms Israel uses in military operations which are not covered by this ban are also used in the settlements. Such laws, which already exist in the UK, the EU, and the United States, have not been barriers to Israel arming itself to the teeth through western largesse. Nothing in Miliband’s statements indicates a fundamental change in that travesty is certain.
The false separation between the Israeli state and Israeli settlements
Israel has long since stopped trying to pretend that the settlement project is not fully part of state activities. The Israeli army openly escorts settlers on their pogroms. The Knesset retroactively legalizes so-called “outposts” that settlers simply put up on Palestinian land. Indeed, the military regularly confiscates Palestinian land, labeling them “closed military zones” or some other title before breaking ground on new settlements there.
Yet Miliband insists on limiting the penalties to the settlements themselves. He intends to sanction ”particularly violent settlers,” but not the Israeli leaders—up to, and including, the prime minister—who enable their activities.
His speech to the House of Commons explaining this “reset” in UK policy toward Israel was prefaced by a long-winded exposition of his love for Israel. But more concerning was his explicit refusal to target the state that is, after all, intentionally pursuing the policies that are bringing these sanctions.
“The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel,” Miliband said. “We will continue to support important and valued trade with green line Israel precisely because we support the two-state solution, including security and prosperity for Israel. For this reason, I wholeheartedly oppose the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions or BDS campaign.”
That strategy is doomed to fail. Beyond the question of enforcement of these new rules, sanctioning the settlements simply doesn’t have much impact. Settlement exports are a very small part of trade between the UK and Israel.
In 2025, according to the UK government’s reports, trade between the two countries totaled approximately $8.1 billion. While it is impossible to know exactly how much trade was done with the settlements because of the evasion practices discussed above, UK records show only about $8 million of imports from Palestine, which includes the West Bank, whatever drips out of Gaza, and the settlements.
Clearly, the trade from settlements is tiny. But the fact is that the settlements are not isolated from Israel. Many firms operating in the settlements are simply parts of larger Israeli companies. Most financing for those companies isn’t specifically sent to a “settlement” business.
Settlers themselves are not worried about this. They know they can find alternative recipients for their goods or, failing that, other ways to make a living. The unending support of the state reassures them, and they’re right to feel that way.
Limited vision
Miliband’s fear of this UK action being seen as a contribution to the BDS movement is also irrational. Whether he likes the movement or not, these are the sort of sanctions BDS activists want to see put in place, although they certainly want them broader, targeted at the state, and with more bite.
His approach to presenting these sanctions reflects another potential flaw in their implementation.
The sanctions were prompted not by a realization that years of UK policy in Palestine and Israel had dismally failed to make any progress toward ending the occupation or stabilizing the region.
No, they were prompted by Israel pushing the envelope, as it has so often done. The government of Benjamin Netanyahu knows well that construction in the E-1 corridor—which would, if completed, bisect the West Bank and shatter the last remaining illusion that a two-state solution is possible—is a red line for the Europeans, and would be so for a more rational American government as well. They also know that the escalated settler violence has prompted negative reactions around the world.
Netanyahu and his cronies are trying to see what they can get away with. Issuing tenders for construction in E-1 is something Israel has threatened to do for decades. They’ve always been forced to back off.
But they have, in the last few years, been able to get away with actions they had previously thought too provocative, such as the complete destruction of Gaza and the genocide of the people there. They have even managed to finally talk the United States into a suicidal war with Iran.
So why not see if they can finally get away with cutting the West Bank in half and putting paid, once and for all, to any Palestinian aspirations for a state?
These sanctions are Britain’s response to that. Even the United States, which routinely screams almost as loud as Israel at any hint of pressure on its Israeli ally, has been relatively quiet about this.
While the Christian Nationalist Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee threatened potential consequences, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who actually matters in this regard, sounded a more conciliatory note: “We heard their arguments as to why,” Rubio said. “But look, we share the goal of stability. We don’t want to see some uptick in violence or an uptick in conflict or tensions in the West Bank at a very tenuous time in the region. But beyond that, as of this moment, we don’t have any further comment.” Neither he nor Donald Trump have said anything more.
This indicates that they are waiting to see if Israel backs off of the construction in E-1 in response to British pressure. There’s a good chance that this will happen, and, if it does, an equally good chance that the UK will back off from its sanctions.
That’s by no means inevitable. By invoking the ethnic cleansing of the West Bank and stating its support for the ICJ’s 2024 ruling, on top of recognizing the State of Palestine last year, the UK has made real progress.
But it’s not irrevocable progress, and Miliband’s own words contain both the promise that something can really change here, and the possibility that Britain will back off, especially if Israel agrees not to take any more steps in E-1 for a while and confines its killing and terrorizing of Palestinians to its security forces instead of the settlers.
Supporters of Palestinian rights—in the UK, the United States, and Europe—can all contribute a lot to pushing the Burnham government forward rather than back. One thing this recent announcement does show is that having been supported by Canada and France, if the UK does take more positive steps, they will be magnified by others.

articles.title: Britain has not seen suppressed American F-35 report
articles.body:
The Ministry of Defence has not had sight of the 2026 edition of the United States Government Accountability Office’s annual report on F-35 production and modernisation, a document the Pentagon has blocked from publication for the first time in more than two decades, according to a written answer published on Friday.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who had asked whether the department had been given access to it. Mr Pollard said: “The Department has not had sight of the 2026 edition of the US Government Accountability Office report entitled F-35 Joint Strike Fighter: Update on Production and Modernization Efforts.”
The report exists and has been completed, but a GAO spokesperson told The Hill in July that it had been reviewed by the U.S. Department of War and marked as containing “Controlled Unclassified Information with no current plan to be released to the public”. The Pentagon declined to comment.
Congress mandated the annual review in statute, and the GAO has reviewed the programme every year for more than two decades, delivering a public verdict each time on cost, schedule, production and readiness. This is the first occasion on which the entire report has been kept from publication.
Controlled Unclassified Information is a handling designation, not a security classification, of course. Material marked that way is not secret in the ordinary sense, but its distribution is restricted, and in this case the restriction extends to a document whose public title has been published while its contents have not.
The 2025 report, the most recent to reach the public, gives a sense of what the withheld edition would have covered. It found that Lockheed Martin delivered 110 aircraft in 2024 and that every one of them was late, by an average of 238 days. Technology Refresh 3, the $1.9 billion suite of hardware and software upgrades on which the Block 4 modernisation depends, was running around three years behind schedule.
On Block 4, the GAO reported previously that the Department of War was redefining the subprogramme and expected it to comprise fewer capabilities than the original plan, deferring development of some to a future effort. The programme had told the GAO in 2018 that it planned to deliver 66 Block 4 capabilities by 2026, and by May 2024 the content had been revised and the completion date extended to 2029. Reporting on the same document put the cost growth at more than $6 billion above original estimates.
The same report carried a Department of War estimate putting the cost of Block 4, engine and power thermal management modernisation, and maintaining and operating the 2,470 planned aircraft across a 77-year life cycle, at more than $2 trillion. The GAO has separately reported that power and cooling shortfalls force the engine to work harder than its contractors intended, reducing its life expectancy, with programme officials estimating that the resulting wear has added $38 billion to the life cycle cost estimate.
What it means for Britain
Britain has been an F-35 partner since the earliest stages, at Level 1 alongside the United States, with British industry holding roughly 15 per cent of the workshare on every aircraft built, on paper at least. BAE Systems manufactures the rear fuselage at Samlesbury, Rolls-Royce produces the lift system for the short take-off and vertical landing variant, and Martin-Baker supplies the ejection seat.
Mr Pollard confirmed on the same day that discussions with the F-35 Joint Program Office are ongoing on procurement profiles and the delivery schedule for Britain’s next batch of aircraft, with delivery anticipated from the early 2030s. The Strategic Defence Review confirmed an intention to buy a further 27 aircraft, of which 12 are to be the F-35A conventional take-off variant to support Britain joining NATO’s dual capable aircraft nuclear mission.
A partner nation committing to further purchases while unable to see the most recent independent audit of the programme’s production performance is an unusual position.

articles.title: Russia uses AI in cyberattacks against Ukraine, Europe, targeting WhatsApp accounts, government ministries, Anthropic says
articles.body:
Russia uses AI in cyberattacks against Ukraine, Europe, targeting WhatsApp accounts, government ministries, Anthropic says
Russia has been using Claude AI in cyberattacks against Ukraine and Europe in recent months, targeting various government ministries and the WhatsApp accounts of high-level officials, Anthropic said in a Sept. 10 report.
"The most commonly recurring targets were members of the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic staff. The actor scanned email services and remote access systems across more than two dozen Ukrainian government organizations," the report read.
Russia has been able to use AI to circumvent defenses against cyberattacks that would be more costly for hackers to do so without the tool.
Russian state-sponsored hacking group Midnight Blizzard "increased their speed by automating their operations using AI" for an actor labelled as GTG-20006 by Anthropic.
"Our attribution is consistent with public reporting linking the actor to Midnight Blizzard. One of the operators is a Russian speaker using the handle 'JackPoterz' whose tradecraft and targeting are consistent with Russian state-nexus espionage," the report read.
Military intelligence targets in Ukraine and Europe, diplomatic and defense organizations, as well as individuals connected to U.S. foreign policy were attacked.
"The actor also took over victims' WhatsApp accounts, using a platform of headless browsers to link victim accounts as companion devices... the actor's configuration suppressed read receipts so victims would not notice while it bulk-exported Russian and Ukrainian language conversations. At least two former high-level Ukrainian officials were targeted in this way."
GTG-20006 used AI to track if known security defenses were evaded and would autonomously modify malware to circumvent existing detections, Anthropic said.
"Our investigation identified more than 20 distinct organizations targeted in the actor's operational planning, reconnaissance, and live operations. They included government ministries, defense and intelligence bodies, embassies and diplomatic missions, think tanks, and defense-industrial companies, concentrated in Ukraine and Europe but extending to the Middle East and maritime-related government agencies in Asia," the report read.
"A common theme of the targeting was Ukraine and military drone technology providers and supply chains."

articles.title: Russian GRU Organized Drone Attack at Leipzig Airport
articles.body:
German investigators have determined that the preparation for the drone attack on Leipzig-Halle Airport was organized by an employee of Russian military intelligence—the GRU.
This was reported by WELT am Sonntag, citing investigation materials.
According to the publication, the suspect arrived in Germany via Turkey and later flew to Serbia. He is currently in Russia, WELT claims.
German intelligence agencies were aware of his probable connection to intelligence services when he entered the country, but did not place him under surveillance at that time.
Back in early September, ZDF reported on two identified suspects, one of whom played an organizational role.
Links between the attack itself and Russian military intelligence had been suggested earlier.
In August, a U.S. intelligence source reported that the explosives and the design of the drone found were characteristic of devices used by the GRU.
As a reminder, the drone carrying explosives was discovered on August 4 near a Ukrainian An-124 transport aircraft at Leipzig-Halle Airport.
The device did not explode; it was defused, and later two more drones were found.
It was previously reported that the An-124 was loaded with ammunition. Subsequently, the German Interior Ministry denied that there were any weapons on board the aircraft.
These events fit into a broader picture described in a report by the U.S. Congressional Research Service. Following the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia expanded its campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks, and other covert operations in Europe.
Weakening European support for Ukraine is cited as one of the possible goals of this campaign.

articles.title: Iraq closes three Iran crossings after drone launch
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq closes three Iran crossings after drone launch
Iraq closed three border crossings with Iran on Saturday, officials told AFP, after a drone attack on a Saudi Arabian pipeline that both Riyadh and Baghdad said was launched from Iraq.
Following the Friday night attack, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed the military commander in Missan province, on the Iran border, after authorities determined that the drones had been launched from there.
Two Iraqi security sources told AFP on Saturday that drone launchers were found near a border crossing in Missan.
No group has claimed responsibility for the attack, and an alliance of powerful Tehran-backed Iraqi armed groups said they hadn't struck the pipeline, though Riyadh has previously accused the groups of targeting its oil infrastructure.
An Iraqi security source and a government official told AFP that authorities ordered the closing of three border crossings with Iran.
The security source said the decision was "part of an intelligence effort to track down the perpetrators and prevent their escape... and to hinder the smuggling of drones through these crossings".
Both sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not allowed to speak to the media, could not specify when the crossings would reopen.
The closed crossings are Shalamsheh in Basra province, al-Shib in Missan and al-Mandali in the central province of Diyala.
Other border crossings with Iran are still open.
A security official said that "security forces found drone launchers near the Iraq-Iran border in the al-Tib" region, a remote part of Missan, close to the al-Shib crossing. A second security source gave the same account.
Zaidi's military spokesperson Sabah al-Numan said the prime minister had approved "Iran's request to conduct a joint investigation into finding drone launch platforms near the Iraq-Iran border".
The government's security media cell said earlier that authorities "have started administrative and security reorganisation operations at several border crossings".
It added that they had stepped up "intelligence activities" to determine "the breaches and violations that took place at these crossings".
It later announced that passengers stranded for hours at two crossings were permitted to pass.
In July, the United States and Saudi Arabia said they had struck Iran-backed militants in Iraq in response to attacks on US forces and Saudi oil facilities.
Pro-Iran armed groups have supported Tehran during the Middle East war, claiming hundreds of attacks on US bases in Iraq and across the region.
On Saturday, those groups, operating under the umbrella of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, said they had not struck the pipeline.
It is "an honour that we do not claim", the Islamic Resistance said in a statement.
Under mounting US pressure, Zaidi has pledged to ensure that armed factions surrender their weapons to the state.
The issue has fuelled tensions in recent weeks, with several groups refusing to disarm.

articles.title: German investigators reportedly link Leipzig airport attack to Russian military intelligence
articles.body:
German investigators reportedly link Leipzig airport attack to Russian military intelligence
German security agencies can now identify with a high degree of probability two suspects following the drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, with one of them linked to Russian military intelligence.
Source: European Pravda, citing German media outlet Welt am Sonntag
Details: Welt am Sonntag gained access in recent weeks to classified, previously unknown investigation materials and spoke to senior security officials.
The editorial team knows the suspects' full names, as well as details of their entry into Germany and departure from the country. This evidence formed the basis for Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt to accuse Russia of carrying out the attack at a joint press conference a week and a half ago. Russia has denied any involvement.
Leipzig/Halle Airport was attacked with an explosive drone on the evening of 4 August. The device was found near a Ukrainian transport aircraft and defused. Investigators found the remains of two more drones near the airport. Security sources said the two main suspects are Belarusian citizen Andrei Ka. and Russian citizen Oleg Le. German security services believe Le. was responsible for planning and logistics for the attack. He is believed to have links to Russian military intelligence.
Investigators say Le. entered Germany via Türkiye through Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER). He later left through the same airport for Serbia. Le. is now in Russia. Welt am Sonntag reported that investigators already knew when he arrived that the Russian citizen is linked to Russia's military intelligence. However, he was not placed under surveillance after entering Germany.
Two of the three drones used in the attack were reportedly destroyed during take-off. The reason for this remains unclear. The third drone reached the Antonov aircraft but failed to explode. Investigators say the plan was to use a total of around 1.8 kg of Semtex explosive. The Antonov aircraft targeted in the attack was carrying about 25,000 litres of kerosene. Investigators believe that had the explosive charge detonated, it would have caused a powerful blast and destroyed part of the airport.
Previously unreleased surveillance footage obtained by Welt am Sonntag shows a drone lying directly next to the Antonov aircraft. Investigators say the explosive device had been hidden in a vegetable tin. The explosion was avoided because the detonator broke off.
The outlet's investigation reveals how investigators tracked down the suspect. Forensic experts found fragments of a glove with traces of DNA on the structure of an antenna which law enforcement officials believe was used to control the drone. These DNA traces had previously been registered in Finland and Lithuania, where Ka. has convictions for ordinary criminal offences. In Finland, he has also been charged with theft, among other offences.
Polish authorities have also linked Ka. to a fire at a DIY store in the city of Łódź, Poland, in the summer of 2024, which prosecutors in Łódź are also treating as sabotage. Polish investigators say the trail in that case also leads to Russia. Ka.'s emergence in connection with the Leipzig attack is seen as further evidence of Russian supervision.
The authorities believe the explosives used in the Leipzig attack probably entered Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia. Investigators believe they were transported in hidden compartments in lorries and later concealed in underground caches. Police found several potential hiding places near Leipzig airport after analysing data from a rented car used by the suspects.
Background:
- It was reported earlier that German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt is planning a package of measures covering protection against drones and sabotage targeting critical infrastructure and cyberattacks, as well as the detection of spies and potential terrorists.
- On 1 September, Germany directly accused Russia of a hybrid attack at Leipzig airport in early August and announced countermeasures.

articles.title: Iran says IAEA chief’s reports helped pave way for US-Israeli attacks
articles.body:
Iran says IAEA chief’s reports helped pave way for US-Israeli attacks
TEHRAN- Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei has accused the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency of helping create a narrative that was later used by the United States and Israel to justify military attacks against Iran.
Speaking at a news conference in Lamerd, a southern Iranian city that was targeted by the United States during the recent war, Baqaei said the IAEA director general’s reports over the past several years had contributed to the emergence of a narrative that Washington and Israel exploited to build a case for attacking Iran.
 
 “Iran’s nuclear program was completely peaceful,” Baqaei said, arguing that “ambiguous and inaccurate” IAEA reports provided grounds for the United States and Israel to justify 'unlawful military action.'
Baqaei said the director general was undermining the credibility of the UN nuclear watchdog through such reports, adding that Iran would continue to demand accountability from both the agency and its director general.
 
 His remarks came as Mohammad Eslami, head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI), traveled to Vienna on Saturday with a delegation of senior officials to attend the 70th General Conference of the IAEA.
Lamerd strike was a war crime
Baqaei also described the US attack on Lamerd as an unequivocal war crime, saying investigations into the strike had established, according to Iranian findings, that a prohibited weapon had been used.
He identified the weapon as a cluster missile and said each munition contained about 180,000 fragments and three-gram pellets.
Standing at the site of the attack, Baqaei said the location was a civilian volleyball stadium where two teenage volleyball players, Helia and Elham, were killed.
He said several teenage football players were also killed at a football field opposite the stadium. A school behind the stadium was heavily damaged, while the Lamerd blood transfusion center was also located in the same area.
“All these sites were civilian facilities,” Baqaei said, adding that three other missiles had struck residential areas.
According to the Iranian spokesman, a total of four missiles hit the city within 35 seconds, leaving the population of Lamerd, a city of around 30,000 people, mourning.
Tehran seeks international investigation and accountability
Baqaei called on the international community, governments and people concerned about human rights to join Iran in seeking justice for those killed in the Lamerd attack.
He also referred to the attack on Minab on the same day, saying 168 people, including students and teachers, were killed.
Baqaei highlighted the case of Avina, a two-year-old child who has become, in his words, a symbol of the civilian toll of the war.
He said Avina represented the “innocence and victimhood” of the Iranian people during 'the US and Israeli military aggression against Iran.'
US. has used prohibited weapons
In a separate part of his remarks, Baqaei said Iran had documented evidence that new and chemical warfare agents were deliberately used in the attack on Lamerd.
He said Washington’s acknowledgment that a new missile had been tested in Lamerd, together with conclusive field evidence and other documentation, contradicted US explanations and demonstrated that the attack on civilians had been deliberate.
Baqaei further added that separate investigations by Iran’s Health Ministry had found that chemical warfare agents were used in the weapons to increase their lethality.
He said all evidence related to a 'war crime' had been documented and would form part of efforts to establish accountability for the attack.

articles.title: An Open Letter from Academics about AI Risk / Life Without the Internet & the Case for Non-Network Redundancy
articles.body:
An Open Letter from Academics about AI Risk / Life Without the Internet & the Case for Non-Network Redundancy
There has been an increase in concern over AI destroying humanity, most recently spurred by tweets from former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon about how dangerous AI is, and a follow-up tweet from current employee Evan Hubinger, who said “Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe A.I. could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”
Some in the AI world are calling for “the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development” and there has been much discussion of trying to slow down or stop all AI research.
Now, a new open letter is circulating, this time from academics worried about the possibility of a “global catastrophe” resulting from AI, calling for political leaders to “create an international treaty, much like the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.” It was written by philosopher Molly Gardner (University of Florida) and made public yesterday. If you’re interested in reading or signing it, it’s here: “Open Letter from Academics Concerning Recent Developments in Artificial Intelligence“.
What follows are some thoughts of mine about one approach to mitigating AI risk. I don’t intend to discourage people from signing the “Open Letter from Academics Concerning Recent Developments in Artificial Intelligence“—it couldn’t hurt to do so.
But for various reasons, I think efforts to slow or pause or stop AI research face an insurmountable collective action problem. Even if the well-known corporations working on AI cease their efforts (itself highly unlikely), research and development will continue. AI tools are relevantly not like nuclear weapons, insofar as work to create and improve them is much less detectable, so enforcement will be extremely difficult or invasive. And since the claims about AI destroying humanity are speculative, the scenarios they describe are unprecedented, and AI is not seen unambiguously as a weapon, there will be insufficient will to implement a regime of punishment (on individuals, corporations, nations) severe enough to effectively enforce cooperation.
I don’t know more about AI than people like Coxon and Hubinger, and while I’m not fully convinced of their pessimism, I haven’t read anything (yet) by other knowledgeable people to show me they’re wrong. So let’s suppose they’re correct to at least this degree: AI poses a serious and pressing risk to the survival of humanity.
What should we do?
Both individually and collectively, we need to develop the means to survive without the internet (and other device and communications networks). Without networked computers, the ability of an AI to do much harm to us decreases dramatically. If we find ourselves imminently facing an AI threat, what we may have to do to save our lives is what many have argued we should do anyway to save our souls: disconnect.
It won’t be easy. This isn’t just about giving up social media, or the hassle of not being able to order things online. And the fact that we all lived without the internet just a few decades ago isn’t all that helpful to us today. Now, every company we rely on for everyday items like food, clothing, shelter, and transportation, every public utility we depend on for things like electricity and clean water, every doctor’s office and hospital, every government agency that’s supposed to provide us with public safety and maintain a good society—they all rely on computer networks. Were we to shut them down, most of these organizations would be barely functional, and the downstream effects of that would be destructive chaos. At that point, AI would be superfluous: we might destroy ourselves.
What we need is non-network redundancy. That is, we need to have in place the means by which to function in a situation in which all of the computer networks have been shut down. By “we” I mean every government agency, every utility, every firm above a certain size, every hospital or medical office, and so on. By “the means” I mean not just plans, schemes, ideas (which some agencies and institutions have), but also the physical infrastructure, the equipment, and the employee know-how to adequately function in the absence of computer networks. (Some government agencies have something like this in place, but not all.) There also needs to be in place the means by which to communicate to the public how to navigate a non-networked world, should that be necessary. Additionally, governments may need to improve their ability to keep track of or monitor potential AI threats, so as to better know if or when it is advisable to pull the plugs.
A demand for action on the AI threat that calls for something highly unlikely to successfully happen may have value as a message to others, including politicians, to pay attention to the problem. But it would be even better if it asked for something useful that can be done. People around the world should be calling on their governments for regulation that requires non-network redundancy.
Will it be easy? No. Will it be cheap? No. But such regulation is of a type that is familiar to people and governments around the world. We have regulatory schemes for workplace safety, for non-discrimination, for accounting, for engineering, and so on. What I’m proposing is a kind of thing we have done before.
This is not a new idea. In some ways it is just an expansion of initiatives like CI Fortify by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), a branch of the Department of Homeland Security.
And it’s not a radical idea. It isn’t a call to ditch computers or to necessarily forgo the benefits that AI may bring. (It’s not a call for a Dune‘s “Butlerian Jihad“.) Rather, it is a form of disaster preparedness.
Does non-network redundancy eliminate all AI risk? Of course not. Eliminating all AI-risk is not possible. Even if there is no further development of the technology, some humans may use existing AI to develop a deadly mass weapon (or something else dangerous, a la “Ice-nine“). (One might note that “eliminate all risk” is not generally a rational regulatory aim for a technology, but we can leave that debate aside.) But, perhaps alongside other measures, widespread non-network redundancy could go a long way toward reducing the risk of catastrophe.
(The foregoing is about non-network redundancy for government agencies, utilities, businesses, and other organizations. What about individuals? Should each of us be ready—really ready—just in case we have to live without the internet? To be honest, I don’t know. Everyone, it seems, should be prepared to weather some kind of emergency. But beyond that, I don’t know what to recommend, or whether it would be a good idea to do much more. For a few reasons, I don’t think a nation of “doomsday preppers” will make for a good society. But it does seem valuable for individuals and communities to be at least discussing these issues.)

articles.title: Xi says China to assume Brics presidency next year
articles.body:
Brics is returning China once again, as President Xi Jinping announced that Beijing will assume the bloc's presidency next year. 
He spoke on Saturday in the Indian capital New Delhi, at the opening of the two-day annual Brics Leaders' Summit.
Xi told the gathering that the 11-member group should "oppose violations of other countries' sovereignty and interference in their internal affairs, (and) constructively participate in resolving hotspot issues," according to Xinhua news agency.
Other leaders attending the summit in the Indian capital include Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, whose country has been at war since US-Israeli strikes against it on February 28.
"As the situation in the Middle East and the Gulf region continues to evolve, the war there has caused serious losses to people across the region," Xi said.
Xi noted that the Brics cooperation mechanism has become world's most influential platform for cooperation among emerging markets and developing countries. He also called on countries to "uphold the authority of the United Nations". 
With Beijing set to assume the bloc's chairmanship in 2027, Xi said China will work with Brics members to play "due role in achieving peace, tranquility in Middle East and Gulf region".
In a joint statement issued on the first day, members of the bloc called for calm in the Middle East.
"We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia and, recalling our respective national positions, call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation," said the statement. 
Meanwhile, Xi also proposed at the conference an initiative on “AI-empowered new industrialisation” designed to deepen collaboration on supply chains. He invited all brics nations to join the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, a Beijing-led initiative aimed at supporting the Global South share AI tools and set fair rules together. articles.title: Romania finds wreckage of several drones on land and in Black Sea
articles.body:
Romania finds wreckage of several drones on land and in Black Sea
The Romanian authorities found the wreckage of multiple UAVs at several locations on 11 September, including some containing warheads.
Source: Digi24, citing the Romanian Ministry of Defence
Details: Drone wreckage was found at several locations in Romania, including around Constanța, in Tulcea County on the border with Ukraine, and in the Black Sea.
Two drone pieces were found on a beach in Tulcea County, while another two were recovered from the Black Sea.
In one case, experts found a warhead and safely neutralised it.
Debris suspected to be from drones found in coastal waters was reported by a commercial vessel, after which border guards located and recovered it. There were no explosives inside.
The latest incident occurred at around 18:00 in a coastal area north of Constanța. Experts from Romania's Ministry of Defence believe the debris came from four UAVs, including an interceptor drone that still contained an unexploded charge. All the wreckage was safely neutralised.
No assumptions have been made about the specific type or origin of the drones.
Background:
- On 10 September, drone wreckage was also found on a beach in Romania.
- On the morning of 11 September, Romania scrambled F-16 fighter jets to monitor aerial assets near the border with Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine Security Service confirms strike on Russian FPV drone production site, warehouses near Taganrog
articles.body:
Overnight September 12, the Security Service of Ukraine, together with the Defense Forces, conducted an operation in the area of Taganrog in Russia's Rostov region, during which it hit a number of important Russian military facilities.
According to a statement of the Security Service of Ukraine on Telegram on Saturday, drones operated by the Security Service's Alpha Special Operations Center successfully struck: two warehouses storing drones; a facility producing FPV drones; a Pantsir-S2 surface-to-air missile and gun system; a tank containing fuel and lubricants; and a P-18 Terek radar.
"Fires were recorded at all the facilities that were hit," the security service said.
"The destruction of drone and FPV drone production and storage facilities limits the ability of Russian troops to use them against Ukraine. This is a direct response to Russia's massive attacks, during which the enemy launches strike drones to terrorize and attack our country's civilian infrastructure," the Security Service of Ukraine said.
