articles.title: Pentagon’s top weapons buyer says Congress must act on munitions
articles.body:
Pentagon’s top weapons buyer says Congress must act on munitions
A top Pentagon official said lawmakers must “step up and deliver” on the Trump administration’s US$1.5 trillion (S$1.9 trillion) funding request if the military is to replenish its stockpiles of key air defence interceptors and deep-strike weapons that have seen heavy use in the Iran war.
“We have the contracts in place, we have the acquisition reform in place,” Michael Duffey, the undersecretary of defence for acquisition and sustainment, said on Sept 11 on Bloomberg Television’s Balance of Power. “We need that funding to deliver for the warfighter.”
Duffey would not speculate on the risk that Congress could decline to finance the Pentagon’s priorities through a party-line budget manoeuvre known as reconciliation.
Regardless of the funding mechanism employed, he said the full US$1.5 trillion is crucial to achieving US President Donald Trump’s objectives.
“It will be incumbent on us to work with Congress over the next couple of months to ensure that we get that full funding for our programme,” Duffey said.
He added that empowering the Pentagon to enter into seven-year production contracts with defence contractors has “incentivised industry to invest their own money” to increase production rates for key munitions.
Asked about the Defense Department’s priorities, he said “we’re focused on the critical munitions that are so essential for our competitive advantage and that are sought after worldwide – weapons like the Patriot, the Tomahawk, the Thaad interceptor, the Standard Missile”.
The administration has announced framework agreements with prime contractors and suppliers of core components for high-end munitions as part of an effort to expand production dramatically in the coming years.
“These investments and these ramp rates will allow us to replenish much faster – expended munitions and also ensuring that we’re building out capacity for the next generation,” Duffey said. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Russian attacks kill six, injure dozens in Ukraine, Moscow says it hits ships, plants
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill six, injure dozens in Ukraine, Moscow says it hits ships, plants
- Russian air strikes in Ukraine on Sept 12 killed six civilians, injured dozens, and damaged homes and infrastructure across several regions including Zhytomyr, Zaporizhzhia, Kryvyi Rih, and Odesa.
- Russia targeted Ukrainian industrial sites like Zaporizhstal steelmaker and ports, while Ukraine struck Russian synthetic rubber plants and warehouses, escalating attacks on critical infrastructure.
- Both sides reported damage to commercial and residential buildings amid ongoing conflict, with local officials confirming casualties and missing persons, highlighting the war's growing toll on civilians and industry.
AI generated
KYIV - Russian air strikes in several Ukrainian regions on Sept 12 killed six people, injured dozens and damaged residential buildings and infrastructure across the country, officials said.
The civilian death toll has risen sharply in Ukraine over the past two months as Russia steps up attacks on power plants and other infrastructure. Ukraine has hit energy facilities and warehouses in distant parts of Russia and both sides have targeted each others’ shipping.
The governor of Ukraine’s Zhytomyr Region, west of Kyiv, Vitaliy Bunechko, said a Russian strike on a grocery store killed two people in the town of Zvyahel. Two petrol stations also came under attack as well as an unidentified “enterprise with foreign investment”, he said.
Earlier, President Volodymyr Zelensky reported attacks on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia and in his home town of Kryvyi Rih.
Zaporizhzhia regional governor Ivan Fedorov said two people were killed and 11 injured in assaults on Zaporizhzhia and other localities.
Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryvyi Rih’s military administration, said two people had been killed in overnight attacks on the city by drones and missiles.
The Russian military said its forces hit Ukrainian steel maker Zaporizhstal in the city of Zaporizhzhia, an Interpipe Steel complex in Dnipro, and several plants in Kryvyi Rih, including the Northern Iron Ore Beneficiation Works complex.
Reuters could not independently verify accounts from either side.
In the Odesa region, governor Oleh Kiper, said 37 people, including an infant, had been injured in a series of overnight attacks. Two people were missing.
The Russian Defence Ministry said Moscow’s forces had maintained their strikes on Ukrainian ports, hitting a cargo ship in Odesa it said was carrying goods for military use.
Earlier in the day, the ministry said its forces had struck two cargo vessels overnight in the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk.
Ukraine’s military said it hit one of Russia’s largest synthetic rubber producers in Togliatti in the Samara region, causing a fire. The Togliattikauchuk plant specialised in the production of synthetic rubbers and fuel additives that are used in fuel for Russian missiles, it said.
Russian regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said industrial facilities in Samara region had been attacked by Ukrainian drones, without specifying which they were or whether they had been damaged, Interfax news agency reported.
Ilya Sukhikh, mayor of the city of Togliatti in Samara region, said several residential buildings were damaged and one person was injured.
In a separate attack, four commercial properties were set ablaze in the city of Taganrog in the Rostov region, local mayor Svetlana Kambulova said, according to TASS. REUTERS

articles.title: EU Examines Funding for Ukraine-Led FREYJA Missile Defense System
articles.body:
The European Commission is examining possible funding for FREYJA, a pan-European anti-ballistic missile project led by Ukraine.
Europe is experiencing a massive shortage of anti-ballistic missiles, as US-made interceptors are currently low in stock due to the war in the Middle East.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
EU Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said on Friday that Brussels could provide “some kind of financial assistance” for FREYJA and other joint EU-Ukrainian defence projects.
According to Kubilius, funding could come from the €90 billion ($104 billion) Ukraine support loan or other instruments, including the €1.5 billion ($1.7 billion) European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP).
Initiated by Ukraine, the FREYJA project was elevated to a European level on the margins of July’s Coalition of the Willing meeting in Paris, with 10 countries now involved.
Executives from Fire Point, Kongsberg, Weibel, Saab, Diehl Defence, Hensoldt, Thales, Safran, Sener and Leonardo met Wednesday in Oslo to coordinate the next steps.
The project aims to combine established European missile-defence components with a cost-effective interceptor being developed in Ukraine.
Freyja aims to deliver concrete results by 2027, although Kubilius gave no broader deployment timeline.
Industry actors have also been cautious, with some being less optimistic, expecting a deployable system in not less than two years.

articles.title: Because of the war with Iran, the United States is not supplying its allies with ATACMS missiles, which Ukraine previously received
articles.body:
Because of the war with Iran, the United States is not supplying its allies with ATACMS missiles, which Ukraine previously received
Kyiv • UNN
Washington is temporarily not supplying its allies with long-range ATACMS missiles because of the war with Iran. Estonia will receive shorter-range HIMARS munitions.
The United States is currently not supplying its allies with long-range ATACMS missiles due to needs related to the war against Iran. Estonia’s Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur said this, ERR reports, writes UNN.
Details
Estonia ordered ammunition for HIMARS systems from Lockheed Martin with ranges of 70 and 300 km. Some of the missiles are already being assembled in the United States before being sent to Estonia; however, the 300-kilometer ATACMS will not be included in this shipment for now.
As for ATACMS ammunition, because of the war with Iran, the American administration has still not authorized its delivery to allies. Therefore, it is currently impossible to obtain them
These are the missiles that the United States supplied to Ukraine
ATACMS are American ground-launched ballistic missiles that are launched, among other systems, from HIMARS. The United States previously supplied such missiles to Ukraine for use against Russian military targets.
Estonia signed a contract to purchase HIMARS back in late 2022, and received its own launchers last spring. According to Pevkur, the shorter-range ammunition may arrive in the country as early as September.
Thus, Washington’s current restriction concerns not only the specific Estonian order, but also the availability of long-range ATACMS for American allies in general.

articles.title: Russia Is Hunting Civilians in Kramatorsk
articles.body:
Kramatorsk is not falling in a single assault. It is being strangled. Russian forces are using first person view (FPV) drones to hunt people in streets and courtyards, dropping guided glide bombs on apartment blocks, and striking vehicles that carry the markings of humanitarian work.
This is not collateral damage. It is a method.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
You do not “accidentally” fly a first-person drone into a vehicle painted with humanitarian markings. You do not accidentally hit a civilian standing in a courtyard when the pilot is purposefully watching and maneuvering a drone towards an innocent victim.
Kramatorsk, like Kherson, is being hunted by drone safaris. Brave humanitarians will still go in and evacuate the elderly, deliver heat and pull the injured out of the rubble, all the while being hunted by soulless drone operators. These are a war crime in plain sight. Document it. Name it. Stop pretending this is just the fog of war.
Drones that see the victim before they kill
FPV drones, including fiber-optic models largely immune to jamming, now operate inside Kramatorsk itself, well behind the line that used to define the “front.” Operators fly them in real time; they see an elderly woman; they choose to kill.
Publicly reported incidents this year include:
• June 6, 2026 – a civilian man killed in a residential area. Ukrainian authorities stated the operator could see the target before impact.
• Sept. 4, 2026 – two civilian cars struck by FPV drones in the city; fires started beside homes.
EU Clears €3.2B Patriot Purchase for Ukraine Under €90B Loan
• Repeated strikes on parked cars, public transport and anyone moving in the open. “Waiter Drones” are left on rooftops overnight and used at first light to attack the unsuspecting.
Ukraine has documented more than 11,000 Russian FPV attacks on civilians nationwide, including double-tap strikes that hit the same site after medics and firefighters arrive.
The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine has already classified the systematic FPV targeting of civilians in Kherson Oblast – known predatorily as “Drone Safaris” – as crimes against humanity. The same pattern is now being recorded across the Donetsk region, including Kramatorsk.
Aftermath of evacuation vehicle destroyed by a drone near Kramatorsk. (Video courtesy Kiwi K.A.R.E)
Glide bombs on homes
Guided aerial bombs – FAB-250s fitted with UMPK kits – are cheap, hard to stop, and used against housing as well as military positions.
• Sept. 9, 2026 – five glide bombs were dropped on Kramatorsk, wounding four civilians (women aged 59, 70 and 74; a man aged 72), damaging 27 private homes and a car.
• Late August – some nine glide bombs hit apartment blocks in Kramatorsk with dozens wounded, including an infant.
• Bridges and crossings have been struck as a warning that the way out can be impeded and ultimately closed.
These strikes sit inside a wider campaign of Shahed-type drones and missiles against Ukraine. Kramatorsk’s daily reality, however, is closer and more personal: an FPV drone patrolling a courtyard; a glide bomb hitting a block of flats; roads that are no longer safe to drive.
Targeting people who come to help
The most damning evidence is the targeting of marked civilian and humanitarian vehicles whose purpose is visible from the air.
To date, the “Road-of-Life” program, which falls under the umbrella of Kiwi K.A.R.E (Kiwi Aid & Refugee Evacuation) charitable trust, has come under enemy fire 11 times with five vehicles completely destroyed: two ambulances, one armored ambulance, and two passenger vehicles. Fortunately, there have been no fatalities however several volunteers have been injured with one person remaining in hospital.
• June 1, 2026 – FPV strike on a clearly marked Civil Protection Department vehicle of the Kramatorsk City Council injuring one official. The city’s military administration called it deliberate as the markings were clearly visible; civilian cars stood nearby.
• Sept. 5, 2026 – a volunteer “Road-of-Life” vehicle was destroyed by a drone attack in Kramatorsk while being loaded for evacuation and aid work.
• Sept. 7-8 – three more “Road-of-Life” vehicles were attacked and destroyed, including an armored ambulance, seriously injuring an evacuation team member who was hospitalized.
• Numerous other missions in the Donetsk-Kharkiv belt has logged well over 100 attacks on staff, vehicles, offices and warehouses.
It is for this reason that humanitarian operations in and around Kramatorsk have become extraordinarily hard: driving under drone nets, detectors are a must in vehicles, teams aborting pickups when a drone threat represents clear and present danger.
Evacuations do still happen albeit with reduced frequency, at a slower pace, and with the recognition of significantly heightened danger. Every kilometer is a calculation.
International humanitarian law requires parties to distinguish civilians from combatants and to spare those who bring aid and conduct evacuations. Russia is doing the opposite – they use attacks on humanitarians as a method of warfare.
A city being emptied on purpose
Kramatorsk still stands. Ukrainian forces still hold it and will for the foreseeable future. But life is leaving. Cafés that were full a year ago are quiet. Supermarket shelves are empty. People stay indoors except for essential movement.
Police and local authorities have said it is time for remaining civilians to leave. Tens of thousands have already been displaced from the Kramatorsk district this year. The method is familiar: isolate the city with drones and bombs, punish movement, hit the rescuers, and wait for the population to drain away.
                                                                                                                                                                         
This is a war crime pattern – not an accident
Kiwi K.A.R.E calls these acts what they are:
• Willful killing and targeting of civilians.
• Attacks on civilian objects and housing.
• Attacks on humanitarian and civil-protection personnel and vehicles displaying distinctive signs.
• Terror against a civilian population to force displacement.
These are prohibited under the Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law. They are being documented, daily, by Ukrainian prosecutors, city authorities, emergency services and independent journalists. The operators who fly a drone into a marked aid vehicle, and those who order the method, must be named and held to account.
What we ask
• Governments and media: treat FPV hunting of civilians and strikes on marked humanitarian vehicles as the war crimes they are – not as “battlefield friction.”
• Donors and partners: frontline aid in Sumy, Donetsk and Kherson is still possible, but only with the equipment, protection and funding levels that match the threat. Well-marked humanitarian vehicles are being destroyed. Replacing them is now a matter of life and death.
• New Zealand and allied governments: sustain political, military and humanitarian support for Ukraine. Isolation of cities like Kramatorsk is a strategy. Silence assists it.

articles.title: Half a million Russian troops killed since start of full-scale invasion of Ukraine, British intel reports
articles.body:
Half a million Russian troops killed since start of full-scale invasion of Ukraine, British intel reports
An estimated 500,000 Russian troops have been killed so far in Moscow's full-scale war against Ukraine, British intelligence officials announced on Sept. 11.
In a prepared statement to journalists, the head of the U.K's military Sir Rich Knighton detailed the loss of Russian troops, Sky News reported.
"I think these numbers illustrate clearly the senseless and futile waste of human life for such little progress, and against such an illegitimate aim of President (Vladimir) Putin," Knighton said.
The majority of Russia's losses occurred since Jan. 2023, Knighton said. In that time, Russia gained only 2% of Ukrainian territory.
The Head of the U.K.'s intelligence, cyber, and security agency, Anne Keast-Butler, previously said that "new intelligence" revealed nearly 500,000 Russian troops had been killed in the war by late May.
Kinighton said that the number of Russian casualties, meaning killed, wounded, and missing, is thought to be 1.5 million since February 2022, matching Ukrainian estimates.
Ukraine's General Staff of the Armed Forces reported on Sept. 11 that Russian casualties, meaning killed, wounded, and missing, now stand at over 1.5 million since the start of the full-scale invasion. The figure includes 1,490 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
The Kremlin's total personnel losses in Ukraine now exceed the combined toll suffered by Russian and Soviet forces in all wars and armed conflicts during the second half of the 20th century and the early 21st century, the General Staff said.
With such a large death toll, Knighton said the war was beginning to impact Russia's economic outlook.
The deaths have "resulted in slowing growth in Russia, weakening consumer demand and stubbornly high inflation, and the cost of Russia's economy and its people's prosperity and prospects are enormous," Knighton said.
Due to heightened inflation risks from Ukrainian drone strikes on oil facilities, the Russian Central Bank's board of directors on Sept. 11 decided to keep the key rate at 14%, the first time the regulator has opted not to cut it since mid-June 2025.
A June 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties from February 2022 to June 2026, of which and 125,000 and 150,000 are thought to be killed in action.

articles.title: Russian strikes reportedly kill four in Ukraine, hit steel plant and residential areas
articles.body:
Russian strikes killed four people overnight in Ukraine, including two at a steel plant in Kryvyi Rih and two others in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, local authorities and the steelmaker said on Saturday.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih said its facility was struck by a Russian missile, killing two people and damaging production facilities.
“We emphasise our plant is a civilian facility in the mining and metallurgical industry, and we strongly condemn these insidious enemy attacks,” the company said in a statement on Telegram.
The attack was part of a wider wave of Russian missile and drone strikes across Ukraine, with civilian infrastructure reportedly among the sites hit.
Residential areas hit in Odessa and Zaporizhzhia
Two people were also killed in Zaporizhzhia after an overnight strike destroyed a house, according to local authorities.
In the southern port city of Odessa, Russian missile and drone attacks struck residential buildings, destroying entire floors and injuring 35 people, regional Governor Oleg Kiper said.
Russia has intensified its long-range missile and drone attacks as its full-scale war on Ukraine, which began in February 2022, enters another period of heightened escalation.
Ukraine has responded with its own long-range strikes inside Russian territory, particularly targeting oil refineries and logistics facilities.
Zelenskyy urges Trump to tighten pressure on Russia
The escalation has contributed to the highest civilian death toll in Ukraine since the early stages of the war, according to Ukrainian officials.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday urged US President Donald Trump to impose “severe” and immediate sanctions on Russia, arguing that tougher measures were needed to restrict Moscow’s ability to produce missiles.
US-led diplomatic efforts to end the war have so far failed to produce a concrete breakthrough, while attacks by both sides continue.

articles.title: Russian president discusses ties, trade with South African, Egyptian, Malaysian leaders
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday held separate meetings with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi, India.
In talks with Ramaphosa, Putin said Russia-South Africa relations are developing successfully, highlighting political dialogue, parliamentary ties and cooperation in education and humanitarian affairs, according to the Kremlin.
He said bilateral trade continues to grow and noted that Russia increased its scholarship quota for South African students to 100 for the 2026-27 academic year.
Putin also said Moscow and Pretoria share similar approaches to major international and regional issues and thanked South Africa for supporting Russian initiatives at the United Nations.
He said Russia is preparing for the third Russia-Africa summit in Moscow on Oct. 28-29, with digital technologies, artificial intelligence, nuclear energy, payment systems and food security among the priorities.
Ramaphosa thanked Putin for supporting South Africa’s G20 presidency and said bilateral trade could be expanded.
He also welcomed continued cooperation and said Pretoria would send a strong delegation to the Russia-Africa summit.
In talks with el-Sisi, Putin said trade between Russia and Egypt is growing and major joint projects are progressing on schedule despite challenges.
He invited el-Sisi to Moscow in October for the Russia-Africa summit and said Egypt’s position on regional and global issues is important to Moscow.
El-Sisi said bilateral trade has surpassed $10 billion and highlighted cooperation on major projects, including the El Dabaa nuclear power plant being built by Russia’s Rosatom.
He also said Egypt relies heavily on grain imports from Russia and Ukraine, making stable supplies a key concern.
El-Sisi said Cairo hopes to work with Moscow and others to promote regional stability.
During a meeting with Ibrahim, Putin said bilateral trade with Malaysia rose 12.9% last year.
The two discussed bilateral cooperation, highlighting growing trade, energy, education, technology and tourism ties.
Putin arrived in India earlier on Friday to attend the 18th BRICS summit taking place on Saturday and Sunday.

articles.title: Yemen government forces say hit Houthis in Red Sea city
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen government forces say hit Houthis in Red Sea city
Yemen's Riyadh-backed government forces said on Saturday they have struck Iran-allied Houthi fighters in the strategic Red Sea city of Mocha.
Following a week-long offensive, the Houthis on Friday captured Yemen's Red Sea coast, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed amid the US-Iran war.
"The armed forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia backed by the Iranian regime," near the port of the city of Mocha, the government news agency Saba reported.
The spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, said they have also struck the Houthis' "vehicles and members" on the Mocha-Dhubab road, 11 kilometres (7 miles) from the city, according to Saba.
Nazili said Friday they had begun shelling areas in Mocha, and called on citizens not to use the Taiz-Mocha and Mocha-Dhubab roads.
The Houthis seized control of Mocha on Thursday, with their attack driving many to flee to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.
On Friday, Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mocha's airport, while a local official said the city's seaport was hit by six missiles of unknown origin.
The Houthi offensive, which started last week, has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.
It has also displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.
It is part of renewed hostilities in Yemen's civil war that began with the group's takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014.

articles.title: Ukraine claims first-ever battle between naval drones
articles.body:
- Ukraine's Navy says its Sargan-3000 drone boat destroyed a Russian uncrewed surface vessel in the Black Sea using a 12.7mm remote weapon turret.
- The Navy called it the first battle in history between two uncrewed naval vessels, though the claim has not been independently verified.
Ukraine’s Navy said one of its Sargan-3000 uncrewed surface vessels destroyed a Russian drone boat in the Black Sea, describing the engagement as the first battle in history between two uncrewed naval vessels.
The Navy said its Defense Intelligence partners spotted the Russian craft before the Sargan-3000 closed in and destroyed it using a remote-controlled 12.7mm machine gun turret known as the Protector RWS.
The Navy’s statement, released on its official channels, did not give a date, exact location or details about which type of Russian drone boat was destroyed.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate, known as HUR, identified the target before the Ukrainian Navy carried out the strike, according to the announcement.
The Sargan-3000 is the same class of Ukrainian drone boat that sank the Russian border patrol ship Izumrud near Gelendzhik in July 2026, one of several Black Sea Fleet vessels Ukraine’s uncrewed boats have destroyed or damaged since the full-scale invasion began. Earlier in the war, similar Ukrainian sea drones sank the missile corvette Ivanovets and the landing ship Caesar Kunikov, part of a campaign that has pushed much of the Black Sea Fleet away from Crimea and back toward Novorossiysk.
In May 2025, a Ukrainian naval drone reportedly shot down a Russian Su-30 fighter jet with an air-to-air missile, another claimed first for uncrewed surface vessels.
Russia has been building its own naval drones in response. A Russian KAMA-type uncrewed surface vessel, built by the Izhevsk-based firm ZALA, was destroyed by Ukrainian forces near Snake Island on September 8, 2026, though in that earlier case Ukraine used a guided munition dropped from an aerial drone rather than a rival boat.
